title: The Cotswolds above Chipping Campden
subject: Landscape
blurb: Working en plein air, Knighton-Hammond would have been painting rapidly to capture the powerful drama of the sky, the source of light in nature, and searching for the most succinct précis of events before him. The rhythm and vitality of his brushwork came to be recognised as his version of Impressionism. The road carries the spectator’s eye into the composition where you come across the horse and cart and beyond to the spirited brushstrokes of the trees and landscape. There is an instinctive feeling for light, colour and tone which enabled Knighton-Hammond to produce this work full of luminosity and clarity. It is clear the artist was fuelled by a profound love of the natural world.

title: A French Square
subject: Streetscape
blurb: This very Impressionistic watercolour of part of a square in France would have been executed en plein air by Knighton-Hammond. Painted directly onto the paper with no under drawing shows confidence and skill. The building has been quickly composed without being slavish to detail yet the suggestion of the architectural elements is perfectly sufficient. The rapidly painted figures and horse give a sense of scale and spontaneity. The majestic trees are imposing and break-up the sunlight producing shade. This is Knighton-Hammond painting with great freedom yet great accuracy.

title: Reeves the Tramp
subject: Portrait
blurb: Mr Reeves, The Tramp appears to have been a frequent visitor to Knighton-Hammond’s studio in Ditchling in the mid-1930s. This small etching may well have derived from a study which he later turned into an oil painting. It may have been the warmth of Knighton-Hammond’s studio which attracted Mr Reeves but there certainly seemed to have been great friendship between artist and sitter. One can imagine the dialog taking place between them during the portrait process.

title: A Continental Market
subject: Streetscape
blurb: This is a very quick watercolour which is delightfully free and sketchy by Knighton-Hammond was painted in a very Impressionist manner. He would have painted the scene on the spot exploiting the light of the Mediterranean and the colours from his paint box. The figures are full of life and spontaneity as they engage in their individual conversations. The artist’s freer style does not slavishly represent detail but is executed with effortless ease and gracefulness. The dog adds to the composition of everyday life in a Continental market.

title: Continental Market Scene
subject: Streetscape
blurb: This complex, multi-figural, busy market scene is full of life and colour with a fierce expression of energy. The ordered watercolour with its dynamic, conspicuous, colliding brushstrokes of vivid colours painted at lightning speed, the absence of ‘drawn’ outlines, creates a light-saturated composition in which not only atmosphere but motion seemed to have been caught and frozen for a moment. Knighton-Hammond’s continental market scenes can be described as a celebration of everyday urban life resulting from his personal understanding of the subject. The artist has focused on the interactions of the crowds and the fact that in each part of the composition a human story is being told powerfully engaging the viewer’s interest.

title: Young Harold Brayne and his parents
subject: Portrait
blurb: The soldier in this picture is Harold Brayne in uniform having joined the army here with his proud parents dated 1939-40. The Brayne family played a major part in supporting the life of the Knighton-Hammond family. At Ditchling, Mr and Mrs Brayne (Nathaniel and Ellen) took on the roles of handyman and housekeeper. As the couple were always on hand they were, along with son Harold, to feature in many of Knighton-Hammond’s paintings. Here the artist captures the character of each of the Brayne family. We are well aware the artist portrayed good likeness of his sitter but he also was a master at demonstrating the psychological likenesses. Each portrait has individuality resulting from his penetrating powers of observation. The composition clearly conveys human presence rather than mere artistic process, important though that is. The rich oil paint, applied as impasto, gives texture particularly to the modelling of the faces and in the articulation of the drapery. Mrs Brayne has a reassuring hand on her son’s shoulder and in turn Mr Brayne has a similarly reassuring hand on his wife’s shoulder. Knighton-Hammond was a master portraying hands with slight exaggerations making for greater expression. When the Knighton-Hammond family moved to Somerset in the latter part of 1940, Mr and Mrs Brayne moved with them. A while later they missed Ditchling so much they moved back.

title: Sailing Boats in Harbour
subject: Coastal Scene
blurb: The harbour would be on the French Riviera, possibly in the Menton area. Whilst the brushstrokes appear to be haphazard in the foreground water, they are part of a profusion of constructive marks depicting the sea and the reflections from the sailing boats. The boats give a range foreshortening effect. The harbour wall breaks the composition with the atmospheric mountains in the background. The use of watercolour shows an instinctive feeling for light, colour and tone producing a work of luminosity and clarity.

title: Harbour view with moored boats
subject: Coastal Scene
blurb: Knighton-Hammond was always in his element when he was able to paint harbour scenes. The light and colour attracted him and his watercolours were ideally suited for him to produce works of luminosity and clarity as with this harbour scene. The majestic sailing boat on the left with its attendant rowing boat have figures going about their business with a stylistic freedom of touch. The light of the Mediterranean in both sky and that reflected in the sea are harmonious in setting the scene. This is yet another good example of Knighton-Hammond portraying everyday life and cleverly elevating it into an art form.

title: Shere, Surrey
subject: Streetscape
blurb: This street scene in Shere near Guildford in Surrey focuses on St James’ Church at the end of the road. The use of watercolour has an instinctive feeling for light, colour and tone producing a work of luminosity and clarity. The absence of ‘drawn’ outlines, creates a light-saturated scene with figures of great spontaneity and their motion captured as a frozen moment in time. Both the architecture, with its precise linear perspective, and the figures show great freedom yet great accuracy. Executed on the spot, the work possesses freshness and immediacy. The foliage of the various trees in greens and browns is rich in form and colour.

title: The Terrace, Haddon Hall
subject: Landscape
blurb: This early watercolour depicts the Upper Terrace at Haddon Hall. It is likely that the work was carried out in the 1890s when the artist was studying at Nottingham School of Art and was a frequent visitor to Haddon. The picture contains an embossed ‘E.S.K.’ stamp standing for ‘Examined South Kensington’. Nottingham School of Art was governed by the South Kensington School of Design. The work may have been submitted for consideration for exhibition at the Royal Academy. The linear perspective of the trees on the rights and the masonry balustrade on the left leads the spectator into and along the terrace. The ground surface of the terrace and the lawn have been broken up with sunlight passing between the trees. The architectural detailing of the balustrade and the Hall indicates Knighton-Hammond had a good grasp of illustration which he would have been taught studying under Wilson Forster at Nottingham School of Art. The foliage of the trees is rich in form and colour. This watercolour shows a young artist with considerable talent and was to go onto bigger and better things.

title: The Font, St Stephen's Crypt, House of Commons
subject: Interior Scene
blurb: This watercolour would date from July 1925 when Knighton-Hammond was briefly back from the continent. He was given consent to work in and about the Houses of Parliament. The artist was in St Stephen’s Crypt when he set himself up with a view of the Font through a gothic aperture with a low-level railing and wrought ironwork scrolls. The covered font is drenched in light contrasting with the dark area adjacent from which he was painting. Knighton-Hammond applied the watercolour with great freedom and fluidity. One has the feeling that the font is admitting light rather than just reflecting it such is its vibrancy.

title: Harvest Time in Youlgreave
subject: Landscape
blurb: This early watercolour by Knighton-Hammond he has adopted the rule of the third’s convention in the composition. The lower third has the corn stacks of the harvesting and most of the action of the farm personal taking place. The middle third contains the architectural elements of the cottages and All Saint’s Church separated by the imposing mature trees. The upper third is the sky with its cloud formation. The figures surrounding or on the fully loaded horse drawn haycart give a sense of scale and movement. This is a very freely painted work with fluid brushstrokes. Further movement is provided by the smoke rising from the chimneys and the birds in flight. Depth in the picture has been achieved with the use of the ‘local’ green and yellow colours in the foreground transforming into the ‘atmospheric’ blue in the background modified by the vail of atmosphere. All-in-all an accomplished, beautiful, harmonious rural scene which the artist enjoyed painting during his stay in Youlgreave c1908.

title: Pont Neuf, Paris
subject: Streetscape
blurb: There is a lot of ink in this etching so it is likely that the artist would have run-off earlier states building up to this final state. The composition is busy demonstrating fine draughtsmanship. The spontaneity of the figures on the nearside bank of the River Seine speaks for itself. The architecture of Pont Neuf and the impressive buildings beyond is a masterclass in linear perspective. The hatching given light and shade is very accomplished. The figures looking over the parapet of the bridge and the street lamps add so much to the composition and are part of the fine tuning of the etching. This is another example of Knighton-Hammond portraying everyday life and cleverly elevating it into an art form.

title: Haymaking
subject: Landscape
blurb: This was a very quickly produced watercolour. It is a little unusual insofar as Knighton-Hammond has drawn in the outlines of the figures, the haymaking machine and some contours of the hayrick in pencil. The girls on the rick and clearly helping the farm operative who is working the machinery. This picture would appear to be Knighton-Hammond having fun with a quick watercolour sketch – so free yet expressive. Some elements of the haymaking machine are incomplete but that didn’t bother the artist.

title: A Busy Street Scene
subject: Streetscape
blurb: This etching was not signed by Knighton-Hammond and it is likely that this was perhaps the first preliminary print run. From this the artist would assess what other work was needed in the etching plate to create other effects to the composition. To get more ink into the plate it is likely that Knighton-Hammond would have reworked more on hatching and thus add tone to the elements. The lively gathering of figures in the street are in conversation creating movement and energy. It is likely that the artist would have worked more on the sky in a later state. The architectural elements are well drawn with linear perspective.

title: Tewkesbury Abbey
subject: Streetscape
blurb: After running off his etchings from his etching press, Knighton-Hammond often retained copies in his studio. Later in life he would takeout an etching and enhance it by adding colour - generally pastel as in this case. He did not hold back when it came to colour. Here he has set the mood of the composition with the strength of colour used. He has created a stormy sky but with a shaft of sunlight illuminating the facades of the buildings which is reflected in the river.

title: A Group of Women
subject: Conversation Piece
blurb: The women in the foreground in conversation and going about their business, form the focal point of the composition. The figures would have been painted at lightning speed in the artist’s ‘shorthand’ yet so effective with the articulated drapery and arrested motion or frozen action. The tall buildings dominate the pictorial space and are painted in an Impressionist manner without detail. Watercolour has been used to exploit its special ability to convey light and space. This is another example of Knighton-Hammond portraying simple, everyday life and cleverly elevating it into an art form.

title: French Harbour Scene
subject: Coastal Scene
blurb: This harbour scene is so full of light and colour. The water is made up of brushstrokes in pure colour giving movement and reflections with an intense vibrancy. The rapid execution on the spot gives the finest Impression of the harbour with its wonderful freshness and immediacy. The boats, moored somewhat haphazardly, are an exercise in foreshortening and perspective. The buildings in the harbour background give the artist his architectural focus in an Impressionist manner. This watercolour shows that Knighton-Hammond was an innovative painter who first and foremost captured realism and naturalism in his compositions but with his Impressionist aesthetic.

title: Christ Church, Oxford
subject: Streetscape
blurb: When Knighton-Hammond visited Oxford in August 1924, he was presented with a feast of emblematic architecture. The artist set himself up in St Aldate’s to paint this watercolour featuring the façade of Tom Gate and Tower of Christ Church. This outstanding building was designed by Sir Christopher Wren and built 1681-82. The Tom Gate and Tower forms the main entrance to the Tom Quad. The streetscape ascending up the hill is a masterclass in linear perspective. The majestic architecture is not heavy on detail but on impression. The street is busy with figures, horse and cart, cycle, pram and dog all going about their business providing spontaneity and movement. The scale of the figures adds to the recession of the composition. The road in shade from the flanking buildings and is interrupted by the horizontal flashes of sunlight from the breaks in the buildings on the left from the intersecting streets Pembroke Square and Pembroke Street off St Aldate’s. A really clever interplay with light and shade. Working on the Continent at this time one can see that Knighton-Hammond is mastering urban streetscapes in an Impressionist style as is evident in this watercolour with his stylistic freedom of touch. The picture is a great achievement in drawing, composition and expressive story-telling.

title: Houses of Parliament
subject: Cityscape
blurb: This earlier watercolour of the Houses of Parliament would date soon after 1900 when Knighton-Hammond moved to London. The Elizabeth Tower (Big Ben) stands tall above the Palace of Westminster on the righthand embankment. Westminster Bridge with is arches spans the River Thames. The river is busy with steam boats and barges. The depth to the pictorial space is achieved with the linear perspective of the river wall, the diminishing scale of the lampposts and trees, and the atmospheric perspective of the grey, foggy environment. The gulls in the foreground give a sense of movement.

title: Roses
subject: Flower Study
blurb: This very freely drawn flower study in pure, direct watercolour would have been painted at speed. As usual with Knighton-Hammond the display has been dishevelled with some stems being placed on the table. The flower heads are not in full bloom but the artist still manages to make the composition of interest. With flower studies the subtle colour variations, tones and shade are essential to get the full effect using watercolour.

title: A Bunch of Roses Painted in Italy
subject: Flower Study
blurb: Knighton-Hammond has made this display of roses less formal by the removal of one of the stems and placing it on the table. The flower heads have been described in watercolour with a profusion of brushstrokes. The green foliage enhances the colour of the pink roses. The background projects the flowers forward onto the table. The picture was exhibited at The Royal Glasgow Institute of the Fine Arts in 1952 (No. 284).

title: A Market Square, San Remo
subject: Cityscape
blurb: Bathed in Mediterranean sunlight, this watercolour has an instinctive feeling for light, colour and tone enabling Knighton-Hammond to produce a work of luminosity and clarity. The market square is delightfully free and sketchy with great fluidity in the application of the paint. Dating from the mid-1920s the work traces the artist’s emerging mastery of urban streetscapes painting in an Impressionist style and shows a deepening understanding of the dynamics of urban life in Italy and France. The large tree and the architecture are important focal points along with the figures and the fact that in each little cluster a human story in being told. The children in particular in the foreground interacting with the adults on the bench are full of spontaneity and movement. The gestures and activities of the figures and horses establish the mood of the scene. The foliage of the tree is painted in very fluid watercolour. This picture demonstrates that the lessons of Impressionism had been fully absorbed by Knighton-Hammond and it is possibly the light that makes the watercolour so brilliantly alive and targets the senses.

title: A Continental Street Scene
subject: Streetscape
blurb: The robust architecture of this Continental street scene would have appealed to Knighton-Hammond and is the focus of the composition. The streetscape is made up with clever linear perspective setting the architecture in convincing pictorial space. The buildings and street are depicted in sunshine and shade, painted with effortless ease and gracefulness. The figures within the building gives a sense of scale and movement.

title: Fishing Boats at Concarneau, France
subject: Coastal Scene
blurb: This busy etching is bursting with information and shows Knighton-Hammond searching for the most succinct précis of events before him. The harbour is full of boats of various types and the quayside have figures going about their business. The architecture of the buildings in the background is brilliantly well portrayed with standout salient details. The figures give a sense of scale, movement and spontaneity and would have been drawn in with the etching needle into the copper plate at great speed and with great confidence. The boats have great perspective and foreshortening placing them in a harbour in convincing pictorial space. The artist gives a hint of movement in the water. The vertical sails add to the overall strength of the composition. Knighton-Hammond was a master of bringing an expression of energy in his etchings from line alone.

title: Flower Study
subject: Flower Study
blurb: This assortment of different flowers is arranged in a blue bowl sitting somewhat uncomfortably on the back of a circular table. The flower heads are laid in with powerful strokes of impasto, in which colour and texture are unhesitatingly defined. For Knighton-Hammond, flowers were a way to explore the interplay between nature and light, capturing the impermanence of life associated with cut stems. The artist’s wife was a very keen flower arranger and would present him with good floral arrangements for him to paint. He, however, did not like the formality so would remove a few flowers and place them on the table. With flower studies its vibrant colours, delicate details and serene compositions can evoke joy, nostalgia and provide inspiration. They remind us of the fleeting nature of life and the beauty that exists in every moment. Perhaps a little surprising but this Knighton-Hammond flower study is very reminiscent of the work of Renoir and other French Impressionists.

title: Amongst the Pines and Heather – Mr Lloyd George’s House at Churt
subject: Landscape
blurb: This picture was undertaken whilst Knighton-Hammond has some spare time painting the portrait of the Right Honourable David Lloyd George at his home in Churt, Surrey in September 1933. The pine trees stand imposingly in the landscape surrounded by foliage which is exceedingly rich in colour and full of vitality. There is a vista through the trees where the eye is drawn to the distant landscape described in atmospheric blue hues. The sticks of pastel have been applied firmly laying on as much of the pastel as possible. The trees are cleverly silhouetted against the sky with the trunks depicting a light and dark contrast. The picture was exhibited at The Pastel Society 1934 (No. 312) and acquired by the Lloyd George family where it had remained until recently.

title: Heath Fires at Churt, Surrey
subject: Landscape
blurb: Whilst Knighton-Hammond was engaged in painting a portrait of the Right Honourable David Lloyd George at his home in Churt, Surrey in September 1933, a heath fire broke out in the evening. Whilst Lloyd George sprang into action directing a large group of men working to control and contain a forest fire, Knighton-Hammond sprang into action with his pastels. The medium was ideally suited to rapidly fix the scene as he first encountered it. The principal structure and tones could be noted in a matter of minutes. The artist has conjured the atmosphere of the hurried actions of the figures and his focus on the fire and smoke creating a scintillating effect of light all captured in strong colours and contrasts. Knighton-Hammond has used the pastel firmly creating thick lines with little or no blending. The artist’s interest in painting in pastel came about a few years earlier from his friendship with architect and artist Edgar Wood. He knew Wood from his time living in the Manchester area in the 1910s, and later as a near neighbour when Wood was living at Porto Maurizio, close to the Franco/Italian border in Italy. Wood was an accomplished artist in pastel and was a good draughtsman which he owed to his architectural skills. Lloyd George acquired the picture from the artist and it remained in the family until recently.

title: The Right Honourable David Lloyd George, OM, MP, 1st Earl of Dwyfor (1863-1945)
subject: Portrait
blurb: This life-size, half-length, three-quarter profile portrait was painted at the sitter’s home in Churt in Surrey in September 1933. One is immediately aware how much thought and technical knowledge have been brought to bear on this pastel of this great statesman and yet there is nothing laboured or heavy in the result. Knighton-Hammond shows us his sheer virtuosity and a capacity for capturing the likeness of this well-known and famous former Prime Minister. Lloyd George was not the most patient of sitters so the artist had to work rapidly. The head is painted with a deceptive simplicity with the light coming from the right and a richness of complexion has been achieved and the long white hair stands out as a Lloyd George trademark. Rich in harmonious modulations the pastels have been blended with the finger tips giving a softness of texture executed with delicacy and control. Whilst the sitter appears slightly uncomfortable in his pose, Knighton-Hammond went beyond capturing the mere physical likeness to achieve a psychological likeness – the human presence, communicating the soul and character of this great man. With some clever handling of the background, the artist projects the sitting into the space of the spectator. The portrait was exhibited at The Pastel Society 1934 (No. 354) before being returned to the Lloyd George family where it had remained until recently.

title: Ploughing
subject: Landscape
blurb: The two powerful working horses pulling the plough are front and centre on this impressive oil painting. This work would date from a period before Knighton-Hammond headed off to the Continent for 10 years in 1922. The Ploughing picture is, therefore, still in a more traditional style before he was influenced by the light and colours of Italy and France. The horses and the attending farmer create movement. To give recession in the composition the artist uses horizontal planes starting with the foreground ploughed field through to the grass in the adjacent field, trees and hedges and the hills in the background. There is a rhythmic division between land and sky. The cloud study interrupts the light from the ever-changing effects of the sky which we are well aware Knighton-Hammond enjoyed painting.

title: Shepherds penning their sheep
subject: Landscape
blurb: The shepherds are corralling their sheep into the pens set in the sloping field. This picture would have been painted at speed by Knighton-Hammond. There is very little, if any, under-drawing so the brush would have been used to paint directly in watercolour. This demonstrates the artist’s total confidence in application which is delightfully free and sketchy but so sure in drawing. Knighton-Hammond has used a very limited palette restricting himself primarily to blues and greens. The figures and sheep have been sketched in with an almost shorthand creating vitality, spontaneity and movement. The landscape is created from spirited brushstrokes with a degree of elegance all of which powerfully engages the spectator’s interest.

title: A Lone Cow by the River
subject: Landscape
blurb: This twilight scene is likely to be in the Lathkil Dale near Youlgreave. The lone cow is being milked by the farmer seated on his stool. The cow nonchalantly is gazing into the bustling river as she gives her milk. There is a single arched bridge spanning the river with buildings on the far side. The subdued lighting of the evening creates a stillness and atmosphere. A small shaft of light is picked out on the cow and on the rapids in the river. The artist takes advantage of the texture of the impasto with its thick, oily, saturated, subdued pigments in rhythmical brushstrokes to bring realism to the composition. Every stroke has been applied with an unerring sense of the total effect at some distance.

title: Fishing on the Pond
subject: Landscape
blurb: This idyllic, tranquil landscape has a lone fisherman in his boat on the pond. The composition is a close descriptive of observed nature full of colour and light. The trees at the side of the pond have decorative foliage very rich in colour, form and full of vitality. The cattle give a sense of scale and movement. When the spectator’s eye escapes the foreground, the background, skilfully half-concealed by trees opens up to the distant hills. The beautiful blue sky creates a scintillating movement of sunshine across the landscape.

title: Ploughing
subject: Landscape
blurb: Knighton-Hammond has skilfully chosen the medium-distance as the focal point of the horses drawing the plough with an onlooker watching the action. There is a fierce expression of energy amid a profusion of constructive brushstrokes. The stormy sky with its changing moods and shifting light adds to the drama creating a stylistic freedom of touch. The artist was able to portray everyday life on the farm with its collective activity and elevate it into an art form in his own clear and distinctive style optimising the aesthetic response to nature.

title: The Derbyshire Dales
subject: Landscape
blurb: This Autumn scene in the Derbyshire Dales is full of atmosphere. The flowing river finding its way around the rugged stones spread throughout. The river is flanked by trees with their tints of Autumn and lead the spectator’s eye to the hills in the background. The depth of the composition is achieved by contrasting the local colour of greens in the foreground through to the atmospheric, hazy blues and purples in the background. From this early landscape one can see a glimpse of the future landscape masterpieces which were to follow in his very long career.

title: Cattle in a landscape
subject: Landscape
blurb: As a small boy the young Arthur used to go out after Sunday School into the fields sketching from nature. This desire remained with him all his life. This watercolour from later in his career shows a lifetime of experience and skill. The composition is made up of dynamic, conspicuous, colliding brushstrokes which target the senses of the spectator. Every stroke of the brush, seemingly so careless, has been evidently well thought out. The use of light and colour have all the features of what the artist had learnt whilst working in the South of France and Italy. Executed en plein air, the picture possesses great freshness and immediacy.

title: Cattle in an extensive landscape
subject: Landscape
blurb: In this clever landscape the cattle grazing on lush grass in the foreground are part enshrined by the imposing trees in the mid-ground. The spectator’s eye in cunningly lead from the foreground through to the half-concealed background through the gap in the trees to the focal point of the hazy, atmospheric distance landscape. Knighton-Hammond’s art was fuelled by his profound love of the natural world which is clearly evident in this impressive oil painting.

title: Gypsy Encampment
subject: Landscape
blurb: This is a scene that Knighton-Hammond could not have passed by without getting his easel and paints out – too good an opportunity to have missed! The Gypsy Encampment on the side of the road consists of a covered wagon and a caravan. Figures are mulling around and the grazing horse is depicted with clever foreshortening. In the foreground the winding road takes the spectator’s eye into the picture where further depth is given to the background by the use of successive planes of colour through to the atmospheric blue on the horizon and into the powerful, dramatic sky all created amid a profusion of constructive brushstrokes. In conjunction with this variety of brushstrokes and texture of thick, impasto paint, Knighton-Hammond adopted a greater intensity in his colours which are rich in harmonious modulations. He has focused on the scintillating movement of sunshine across the landscape creating a feeling of atmosphere. This powerful composition presumes, indeed solicits, the attention of the spectator as one’s eye is guided around this spectacular art work. Probably painted in the 1930s this picture is Knighton-Hammond at his best – simply brilliant with all the characteristics of French pleinairism and Impressionism. There is a feeling of life in the paint and in the painting.

title: The Meet
subject: Hunting Scene
blurb: This early watercolour dating from the early 1900s has the gathering of the hunt with mounted Huntsmen, support riders and hounds by a historic thatched building. The composition is focused on the interaction of the figures and the quickly applied brushstrokes give the painterly illusion of movement and spontaneity. It is likely, however, that this watercolour was produced on the kitchen table as opposed to on the spot.

title: Huntsmen leading Hounds to cover
subject: Hunting Scene
blurb: This early hunting scene would date from c1901/2 and is likely to have been executed on the kitchen table possibly from sketches. During the early 1900s when Knighton-Hammond was living in London times were tough. In order to pay the rent, the artist used to produce hunting and sporting scenes which he referred to as ‘pot boilers’. He would sell the watercolours through Fores of Piccadilly. The work clearly demonstrates that from early in his career Knighton-Hammond had a good grasp of foreshortening with the horses and hounds moving towards the spectator.

title: Mary, the artist’s daughter
subject: Portrait
blurb: This sketch of Mary, the artist’s daughter knitting or doing some other craft would have been executed at speed. For Knighton-Hammond drawing was a constant study and consideration and one gets the sense it was a source of creative joy. It was likely that Mary was at home relaxing and going about her task when her father, who always had a sketchbook about his person, set out producing this drawing and with a few deft strokes of the chalk set her in a defined and convincing pictorial space. Knighton-Hammond’s drawing practice was speedy and economical in development. With red chalk one could achieve a softness of stroke which reflected a synthesis between line, light and shadow. It is clear the artist was wholly immersed in his art – simultaneously, spontaneous and inventive.

title: Pendomer Church 1951
subject: Landscape
blurb: The 14th century Church of St Roch, Pendomer in Somerset was painted by Knighton-Hammond in 1951. The main focus of the church is the east gable end with its arched window and ham stone dressings. The architecture of the church and the adjacent thatched cottage is painted with a stylistic freedom of touch in watercolour. The churchyard is depicted in fluid colour washes. The tree foliage adds a further touch of colour. The artist uses light to good effect with the gable end of the church in shadow contrasting with the cottage bathed in sunlight. The whole composition would have been executed at speed as was Knighton-Hammond’s way.

title: A Venetian Canal
subject: Cityscape
blurb: This narrow canal in Venice is a master class in linear perspective. The tall buildings flanking the canal are superbly drawn depicting the architectural details. The palace on the right and the church beyond are bathed in sunlight whereas the buildings on the left are in shadow indicated by the levels of ink in the etching. The heavier the hatching the more ink is transferred onto the paper giving the darker image. The artist picks out the salient architectural details only on the building in sunlight. There are a number of gondolas on the shaded canal travelling through the reflective water.

title: Roses
subject: Flower Study
blurb: This flower study of roses in a glass vase is clearly defined and fresh, using colourful, fluid strokes. There is great delicacy and control leading to effortless ease and gracefulness. Later in life Knighton-Hammond enjoyed painting still life subjects in his studio. He used to breakup the formality of flower studies by having at least one of the blossoms loose of the table.

title: Landscape
subject: Landscape
blurb: This landscape targets the senses. The colourful foliage, rich in form, in the foreground is painted with fluid strokes of watercolour. As the eye escapes to the background beyond we see Knighton-Hammond has characterised Impressionism by rendering not a faithful landscape but more the sensation produced by a landscape with its atmospheric blue. The bright composition is lit by a dramatic sky with its colliding clouds.

title: Sailing Boats in Harbour
subject: Coastal Scene
blurb: This watercolour of a harbour is probably Concarneau in France. The busy scene has a sailing boat front and centre with figures in a rowing boat alongside. The masts of the sailing boat are built up with a profusion of constructive brushstrokes creating a fierce expression of energy. The figures in the boats and on the harbour wall, give a sense of scale and movement. The work is delightfully free and sketchy but so sure in drawing and has the right use of colour. The reflections of the boats in the water have great fluidity. The view has a sense of engagement with this composition.

title: The Bridge at Sospel
subject: Landscape
blurb: The Pont-Vieux (Old Bridge) dates from the 13th century and spans the River Bévéra. This is one of a number of pictures Knighton-Hammond painted of this iconic bridge. Sospel is a beautiful little town up in the Maritime Alps on the salt route between Nice and Turin. The picturesque qualities of the town would have been a major attraction for the artist. In the 1920s when this watercolour was painted the journey would have involved a bus ride from Knighton-Hammond’s home in Cap Martin along the Mediterranean coast to nearby Menton followed by an adventurous trip 15km north up into the Alps to Sospel. The journey backdown the Alps from Sospel is a little scary today with modern public transport so in Knighton-Hammond’s time around the hairpin bends on the sides of mountains would have been nail biting! Executed en plein air the artist exploits the special qualities of watercolour to convey light and space. Primarily this is an architectural study where the elements combine great freedom with great accuracy.

title: Pont Neuf, Paris
subject: Cityscape
blurb: This is an early etching dated 1913 by Knighton-Hammond of Pont Neuf, Paris. There are cargo boats in the River Seine being loaded or unloading from a horse and cart on the river bank. The artist cleverly gives depth to the composition with foreshortening of the boats and the view through the arch of the bridge. The figures on the bridge give a sense of scale and movement.

title: The Banqueting Hall, Haddon Hall
subject: Interior Scene
blurb: This sketch has two authentic signatures. On the left is a very early signature – A.H.Hammond - dating from the 1890s when Knighton-Hammond was on a painting holiday from his job as a watchmaker. The other signature Arthur Hammond on the right would date from the second half of the 1900s. The composition has the budding young artist developing his draughtsmanship skills which he enhanced with watercolour. The geometry work at Nottingham School of Art set him in good stead for his emerging career. The inscribed gold mount is original.

title: Ventimiglia, Imperia, Italy, 1930
subject: Landscape
blurb: This colourful pastel shows figures by the side of the River Roya in Ventimiglia. Knighton-Hammond’s interest in working in pastels came about as the result of his friendship with the Manchester architect, Edgar Wood. Wood was living close by at Monte Calvario, Porto Maurizio in Italy and as an artist he worked extensively in pastel. Working in pastel allowed Knighton-Hammond to work rapidly and fix the scene before him. He was able to improvise textures and transitions of colour whilst maintaining the vibrancy of this work. He cleverly blends and softened the pastel blurring the edges with his fingertips. The figures and the Roya estuary give great movement to the composition. The spectator’s eye is immediately drawn to the impressive Alps in the background and experience the brilliant light of the Mediterranean.

title: Little Port, Puglia, Italy
subject: Coastal Scene
blurb: The harbour side buildings are bathed in bright sunlight and are depicted with the accurate perspective we have come to expect from Knighton-Hammond. The trees bring a splash of rich green to the predominately pastel colours. The boats and barrels are out of the water on a sloping stepped ramp way docking area between the harbour wall and the water line. The use of watercolour allows Knighton-Hammond to exploit its special ability of conveying light and space. The boats and barrels show skilful perspective and foreshortening.

title: A quay side study with figures and fishing boats
subject: Coastal Scene
blurb: This busy harbour scene would have been painted on the spot and at great speed in pure direct watercolour. The picture is bursting with information. There is a mixture of sailing and steam powered boats in the harbour. The quay receding away from the spectator gives depth to the picture. The figures have great spontaneity as they walk towards the spectator. The smoke from the boat’s boilers breaks up the sky adding movement to the composition. There is an interesting structure on the harbour on the right. The composition is very freely painted with great immediacy and spirited brushwork.

title: Farm building in a stormy landscape
subject: Landscape
blurb: Knighton-Hammond was inspired by rushing skies, changing moods and shifting light. This storm in watercolour shows simplicity and directness of statement for which the medium is particularly adapted and executed with fierce expression of energy. The free and sketchy composition with the rendering of colour, light and atmosphere has created a more inward depth rather than spaciousness. The trees and building are silhouetted against the stormy sky.

title: Landscape
subject: Landscape
blurb: This landscape would have been Knighton-Hammond experimenting with rapid, fluid brush strokes. Painted in pure, direct watercolour the wet track draws the spectator’s eye into the picture. The trees are silhouetted against the calm sky. This is very much a picture produced to keep the artist’s hand in and possibly warming up for a more extensive composition.

title: June Morning 1955
subject: Landscape
blurb: Dominated by the dramatic sky, this landscape is depicted from a low vantage point. About a quarter of the picture scene is taken up by the flat fields created from a profusion of constructive brush strokes and colours. The cloud study shows the artist in full flow with the rapid notation of the ever moving, mood changing sky.

title: Sailing boats at the quayside
subject: Boating Scene
blurb: The harbour may possibly be Oneglia just over the France/Italian border in Italy in the Imperia area. The masts divide up the composition with their verticality. When your eyes escape the masts, you are drawn to the imposing buildings on the far side of the harbour. These have been depicted in a very free manner not slavishly representing detail. This picture would have been painted at great speed and with great energy, as is Knighton-Hammond’s way with artistic expression. There is fluidity in the handling of the watercolours and would have been painted on the spot, en plein air.

title: Broadway, Worcestershire
subject: Landscape
blurb: Knighton-Hammond set himself elevated above the town at the roadside to paint this panoramic view. There is much going on in this composition and the spectator’s eye is guided around the artwork looking at the chickens in the foreground, following the road down the hill observing the lively figures, the local vernacular architecture of the buildings and church, the landscape in the background and returning to the seated figure on the right adjacent to the boundary wall. The artist uses clean washes of colour to achieve light, space and maximum luminosity, the technique which he perfected, giving this watercolour a clear and distinctive style. There is a brilliant rendition of the construction materials of the buildings and the high boundary wall. Executed with delicacy and control, one feels the artist was wholly immersed in his art which was fuelled by a profound love of the natural world.

title: Fishing Boats in Harbour
subject: Boating Scene
blurb: This harbour scene has an instinctive feeling for light, colour and tone using watercolour to produce a work of luminosity and clarity and rich in harmonious modulations. The boats are wonderfully depicted and it is clear the composition was only possible due to the technical virtuosity of the artist’s draughtsmanship. The masts and riggings are drawn directly with the brush in watercolour - a sign of supreme confidence and sure hand. The sailing boats beached in the harbour and the attending figures are bursting with information and only when your eyes escape the dynamic scene do you then begin to appreciate the domed building on the far side of the harbour. This is a work that targets the senses.

title: A Square in Venice
subject: Streetscape
blurb: Architectural squares acted as a magnet drawing Knighton-Hammond in with his draughtsmanship and watercolour skills. He had the remarkable ability to illustrate buildings with skilful linear perspective and brilliant rendition of façades and in this case with their stucco finishes and architectural details. The buildings here show Venetian Gothic style influenced by Byzantine and Ottoman empires reflecting Venice’s trading network. This is particularly evident in the Islamic window design in the facing window on the left. The geometry of the picture is immediately evident, based on the verticals, horizontals and perspective lines of the architecture. The lone figure brings a sense of scale to the composition. It is a little unusual to depict such a quiet scene as Knighton-Hammond appeared to favour the hustle and bustle of busy urban streetscapes. Whether quiet or busy, these squares and markets added to Knighton-Hammond’s emerging mastery of the dynamics of urban life in Italy and France. The composition shows a stylistic freedom of touch in the hands of a very competent Impressionist.

title: Cattle in a landscape
subject: Landscape
blurb: The most striking thing about this watercolour is the depiction of the trees. Devoid of their leaves, the trees have been wonderfully constructed directly with the brush silhouetted against the sky. Equally as striking are the two cattle in the right foreground captured looking intensely and amusingly at the artist at work. One has the feeling that there is a conversation going on with one of them saying ‘what’s that bloke doing sitting in our field – he’s not the farmer?’ The one on the left of the two shows a good example of foreshortening as it faces out to the spectator. It is likely that this field is on one of the farms in Misterton close to Knighton-Hammond’s home at Old Court and would date from the 1940s or 50s. Picture depth is created using local colour of greens in the foreground receding to a hazy blue/grey in the background. The field in the foreground is depicted amid a profusion of constructive brushstrokes. Knighton-Hammond had great ability to elevate a landscape with cattle into a real art form.

title: The Serpentine, Hyde Park, London
subject: Landscape
blurb: The moody sky sets the atmosphere for this watercolour of the Serpentine in Hyde Park. Knighton-Hammond would have painted this work in the mid to late 1920s when he would have been on a visit home from the Continent. The colliding brushstrokes in the rapid notation of the clouds creates drama. One feels the sun is beginning to break through. The foliage of the trees is rich in colour and form. The artist achieves picture depth through successive planes – foreground grass, The Serpentine, the trees and building on the far side of the water and the extensive sky give a gentle rhythmic division between the natural elements. This leisure scene which would have been painted at lightning speed and is populated with elegant strolling figures out enjoying the park which gives scale and spontaneity to the composition. Knighton-Hammond’s work is delightfully free and sketchy, but so evidently well thought out and the artist’s sure hand enables him to indicate form, colour and transparency with a sweep of his brush.

title: Tom Gate, Christ Church, Oxford
subject: Streetscape
blurb: Tom Gate is the bell tower (Tom Tower) at Christ Church, Oxford. Located on St Aldates. It forms the main entrance to Tom Quad viewable through the entrance arch. This iconic structure was designed by Sir Christopher Wren and built 1681-82. Knighton-Hammond set himself up across St Aldates in Pembroke Square to paint this watercolour. The artist was making trips back to England and we know he had a painting expedition to Oxford in August 1924, when it was likely that this work was undertaken. The emblematic architecture of Oxford presented amazing opportunities for Knighton-Hammond with his skills in depicting buildings with linear perspective, the rendition of the masonry façade and the Impressionist techniques he was learning whilst working on the Continent. This is evident here with the fluidity of brushwork and not working slavishly representing detail but concentrating on the overall effect. The quickly applied brushstrokes in the depiction of the busy figures, horse and trap and car giving the painterly illusion of movement and spontaneity. Knighton-Hammond had an instinctive feeling for light and colour and with watercolour he was able to exploit its special ability to achieve this.

title: A Working Cocker Spaniel
subject: Portrait
blurb: This portrait of a black and tan working cocker spaniel would date from the early 1900s. An unusual subject for Knighton-Hammond even in his formative years. I have had to solicit help with regards to the dog! Painted from life, it would have been quite a task for the spaniel to have stayed still for any length of time. I am advised that the dog’s owner would have been present alongside the artist to issue the command for the dog to remain still. Also, it is likely that the dog was in his own surroundings as opposed to Knighton-Hammond’s studio – that doesn’t mean to say that Knighton-Hammond was in the ‘doghouse’ more likely the gamekeeper’s house! One senses that the spaniel is desperate to be up and about sniffing anything and everything! It is very alert and would be off in an instant if commanded. Knighton-Hammond captured the arrested motion or frozen action of the spaniel poised ready to off in a flash. As a dog portrait this is a very accomplished oil painting. The texture of the paint is used to portrait the dog’s fur. Whilst there is little colour contrast between the dog and the background, Knighton-Hammond has still managed to achieve the disposition of space from the background projecting the dog forward into its own space. There is little doubt that the artist has accurately depicted the physical appearance of the spaniel but he has further captured the endearing character of the dog. There is an element of sentimentality in the dog’s expression being man’s best friend. Even in this early stage of his career, the artist demonstrates his amazing ability to find character in all his subjects.

title: A Mediterranean Bay
subject: Coastal Scene
blurb: Knighton-Hammond presented the coast from dramatic viewpoints and unexpected angles. In this watercolour he is high on a cliff giving a sense of his own excitement as he discovered the beauties of the sites. The view of the peninsula, possibly Cap Martin, is framed by trees which are decorative in foliage very rich in form and colour. The strong Mediterranean light and parched terrain is so typical of the French Riviera. The remarkable special organisation of this picture shows Knighton-Hammond’s interest in the study of light and atmospheric effects.

title: Flower Study
subject: Flower Study
blurb: Still life is, in large part, a salute to life – a celebration. This flower study was probably Knighton-Hammond amusing himself in his studio in later life. He enjoyed having flower arrangements in his studio, normally set up by his third wife and then dishevelled by the artist to lose the formality. Often, he would remove a flower or two from the arrangement and place them on the table adjacent the vase. The flowers, possibly white chrysanthemums, are well painted and there is disposition of space between the blossoms. There is also space behind the arrangement to the wall. Subtle brushwork gives modelling to the blossoms which is clever when depicting a monochrome subject.

title: Cattle in a landscape, Misterton
subject: Landscape
blurb: Knighton-Hammond was always happy to be out painting in the fields of local farms. He knew the farm owners well, most of them featured in his paintings. He was, therefore, always welcome on their land and his presence caused them amusement and pleasure. His art is fuelled by a profound love of nature. The cattle here are grazing and painted with spirited brush strokes – quick and vibrant. There is a power and energy in the structuring of the animals. Quickly applied brushstrokes give the painterly illusion of movement and spontaneity. The sky is dramatic giving luminosity to the composition.

title: Bale’s Farm, Misterton
subject: Landscape
blurb: This watercolour is delightfully free and sketchy but so sure in drawing. The hillside leads our eyes into the composition the focal points being the cattle. Knighton-Hammond’s feeling for light and colour enabled him to produce works of luminosity and clarity. The cattle are meandering and the one second from the right appearing to be looking around the tree inquisitively at the artist at work. The cattle show clever foreshortening. The trees stand majestically on top of the hill. This type of landscape, which engages with everyday subjects, appears to deliberately minimise human presence to optimise the aesthetic response to nature.

title: Druid’s Hill, Misterton
subject: Landscape
blurb: This watercolour, painted with great fluidity, is distinguished in technique by previously unparalleled freedom of handling. With masses of colour, which when looked into at close quarters seem to resolve themselves into a chaos of pigments, but in which every stroke has been applied with an unerring sense of total effect at some distance. The cattle are just meandering or lying down with the one on the left appearing to look inquisitively at the artist at work. The trees are synonymous with Druids Hill, so called because local legend has it, that it was where Druids held their services.

title: Butter Market, Concarneau, 1930
subject: Interior Scene
blurb: This interior scene of the Butter Market at Concarneau is bursting with life. The figures are full of spontaneity and are deep in conversation. The composition would have been painted at lightning speed with great freedom and great accuracy. Every stroke of the brush, seemingly so careless, has been evidently well thought out giving the painterly illusion of movement. Focused on interaction, Knighton-Hammond creates atmosphere in the interior with a stylistic freedom of touch.

title: The Wye Bridge and Hereford Cathedral
subject: Landscape
blurb: The ‘Old Wye Bridge’ is a 15th century structure across the River Wye in Hereford. It has a long history being rebuilt in the 17th century and widened in 1826. The historic cathedral was begun in 1079 and has substantial parts of the building dating from both Norman and Gothic periods. This watercolour by Knighton-Hammond was early in his career. It shows he had a good understanding of perspective as evident in the architecture of the cathedral, bridge and buildings which are painted with great freedom yet great accuracy. The foliage of the trees, bushes and grass are painted with great fluidity. The reflections from the River Wye are executed to achieve movement in the water.

title: Ditchling
subject: Streetscape
blurb: For this watercolour, Knighton-Hammond set himself up in Lewes Road looking towards the crossroads and West Street beyond. The spire of St Margaret’s Church can be seen standing proudly on the right. Historic Ditchling is built up of varying periods and styles of architecture which the artist depicts with its linear perspective, the brilliant rendition of brickwork, masonry, stucco, timber frame, tiles and slate. The figures going about their business give scale, movement and spontaneity to the composition. A bus is parked up waiting for its passengers. Executed on the spot with watercolours, Knighton-Hammond exploits its special ability to convey light and space.

title: Landscape with a pond
subject: Landscape
blurb: One senses Knighton-Hammond worked rapidly to fix the scene before him. He used the small, easily manipulated sticks of pastel with their granular softness to develop the composition. He created texture and transitions of strong hue blurring the edges where necessary with his finger tips and adding streaks of light as the sun illuminated the roofs of the buildings. Knighton-Hammond focused on the scintillating movement of sunshine across the landscape. The light from the dramatic sky is reflected in the pond which further evokes the brightness of the day and the strength of his colours.

title: Landscape with river with a village beyond
subject: Landscape
blurb: The spectator’s eye is drawn into this watercolour via the bend in the river. The mature trees are rich in colour and painted with fluidity. There appears to be a manor house on the edge of the village. The church stands tall with the tower silhouetted against the sky. It also has been cleverly depicted in the reflections in the water along with the large trees. The stormy sky adds drama to this very accomplished composition.

title: Ploughing
subject: Landscape
blurb: This oil painting in dominated by the two horses waiting patiently whilst the farm operative takes a break. They are full harnessed ready to continue ploughing. The powerful heavy horses are brilliantly depicted with clever modelling giving them their robust, solid, muscular stature. Once the spectator sees beyond the horses, the artist gives depth to the composition through its successive horizontal planes of colour depicting fields, trees and the atmospheric blues of the background blending into the sky. The study of light enhanced by the texture of the impasto oil paint lifts this scene of everyday rural life to something quite special.

title: ‘The Light that Lingers in the West’
subject: Landscape
blurb: This view of a tree-lined valley with a river is in the Derbyshire Dales and given the title of ‘The Light that Lingers in the West’ by the artist. Trees have been recently felled with the trunks laying on the hillside. Figures are mingling around the trunks. The foliage is rich in colour and texture created by the use of thick, impasto paint. The spectator’s eye is drawn through the valley to the atmospheric hills beyond.

title: Tug Boat and Crane at Portside in America
subject: Coastal Scene
blurb: This harbour scene would have been painted when Knighton-Hammond was returning from a 6-month commission for the Dow Chemical Company in Midland, Michigan, USA in 1920. The stream powered tug boat is moored in harbour. The industrial cranes are present to unload cargo. There is an interesting mix of buildings and structures beyond the harbour. The smoke from the funnels gives a sense of movement to the composition. In conjunction with the variety of brushstroke and texture of paint, Knighton-Hammond adopts a greater intensity in his colours. The absence of human presence does not detract from the everyday collective activity as it still powerfully engages the spectator’s interest. This oil painting was purchased by the present owner direct from the artist’s studio in 1968.

title: Sailing Boats in Port in America
subject: Coastal Scene
blurb: This harbour scene would have been painted when Knighton-Hammond was returning from a 6-month commission for the Dow Chemical Company in Midland, Michigan, USA in 1920. Sailing boats are moored up against the harbour wall. The somewhat bleak scene beyond the harbour includes commercial buildings serviced by the cargo boats. The sails giving a lighter colour to the composition. The artist creates a sense of movement in the reflections painted in thick impasto paint in the choppy water. This oil painting was purchased by the present owner direct from the artist’s studio in 1968.

title: Welsh Farmyard, 1910
subject: Landscape
blurb: This farmyard dating from 1910 is likely to be in North Wales when Knighton-Hammond was staying in Colwyn Bay. The young farmworker is surrounded by chickens and appears to have an egg basket tucked under his left arm. The brood of chickens appear lively, colourful and solicits the attention of the spectator. The free handling of the quickly applied paint gives the painterly illusion of movement and spontaneity. The farm buildings have accurate linear perspective and the rugged stonework is so well depicted. This oil painting was purchased by the present owner direct from the artist’s studio in 1968.

title: Statues in Florence
subject: Cityscape
blurb: Knighton-Hammond set himself up inside the Loggia dei Lanzi in Florence to paint Pereus with the Head of Medusa (1545-1554) by Benvenuto Cellini (1500-1571). This impressive statue in bronze is silhouetted against the façade of the Palazzo della Signoria. The work was commissioned by Cosimo I de’Medici, Grand Duke of Tuscany. Out in the Piazza della Signoria is the iconic marble sculpture of David (1501-1504) by Michelangelo (1475-1564). The artist has not concentrated on detail but gives us an impression of the statues. The scale of these works can be gauged by the size of the figures mingling in the palazzo. (Michelangelo’s David stands 5.17m tall – this is a copy with the original in the Galleria dell’Accademia, Florence). By not giving us any detail in the façade of the palazzo the spectator can focus of the statues painted with a stylistic freedom of touch with effortless ease, gracefulness and fluidity yet with a powerful sense of authority. Seemingly unfinished, the work gives an insight into the creative process – a window into the mind of the artist. One can sense the attendant figures are focussed on interaction with these iconic renaissance masterpieces. This watercolour was purchased by the present owner direct from the artist’s studio in 1968.

title: A Bridge in Venice
subject: Coastal Scene
blurb: Just a picture of some boats and a single arched bridge in Venice yet it is bursting with life. With thick impasto there is a feeling of life in the paint and in the painting. The composition is made up with a profusion of constructive, visible brush strokes. The thickly applied daubs of pigment have bold accents of light and shadow very much in the style of the Impressionists. The boats are moored to the side of the canal preparing to off-load their cargo. The figures provide movement. The position of the boats called for clever foreshortening and there is skilful rendering of depth to the view under the bridge.

title: Farm House and Church
subject: Landscape
blurb: This watercolour is full of the techniques learnt from the Impressionists from Knighton-Hammond’s time working on the Continent with his stylistic freedom of touch. The houses and farm buildings have all the architectural features of the Somerset vernacular. We have a master class in linear perspective and a superb rendition of masonry and thatch. The elevated church is bathed in bright sunlight. The foliage is rich in colour and texture. The figures and geese give movement to the composition. He uses motifs to add to the realism of the space with the water trough and the partially open gate. This watercolour was purchased by the present owner direct from the artist’s studio in 1968.

title: I Stood in Venice
subject: Cityscape
blurb: The artist gave this painting the title ‘I Stood in Venice’. The canal is busy with gondolas and also sailing boats moored at the quayside. The line of buildings flanking the far side of the canal have fine linear perspective and a brilliant rendition of the stucco façades. Knighton-Hammond has not worked on detail but provides us with an impression which is perfectly adequate for the architecture to be read. The figures on the quayside trigger awareness of what is going on in the scene and focuses our interaction. The composition guides the spectator’s eye around the art work from quayside to along the façades and back to the figures going about their business. It is completely evident that the lessons of Impressionism had been absorbed fully by Knighton-Hammond. The element of spontaneity has been fully integrated into the process. Light was the principal agent for the Impressionists and Knighton-Hammond uses the ever-changing effects from the sky to highlight the architecture and the water on the canal. The painting was exhibited at the Atkinson Gallery, Stockport 1950 at their 59th Spring Exhibition of Modern Art (No. 188). This oil painting was purchased by the present owner direct from the artist’s studio in 1968.

title: Herring Drifters near Yarmouth
subject: Coastal Scene
blurb: Great Yarmouth was the epicentre of the herring fishing industry. Here Knighton-Hammond shows the herring drifter fleet returning to the quayside. This oil painting was exhibited at the Royal Institute of Oil Painters 1939 in their 56th Annual Exhibition (Exhibit No. 63). There appears to be a combination of sailing and steam drifters in harbour. In conjunction with this variety of visible brushstrokes and texture of paint, Knighton-Hammond adopted a greater intensity in his colours. He used the brushstrokes to evoke the shimmering light reflecting of the sea. The composition is exceedingly rich in colour and full of vitality. Every stroke of the brush, seemingly so careless, has been evidently well thought out and the artist’s sure hand enables him to indicate form, colour and dappled light as the sun shines through the clouds. Amid a profusion of constructive, powerful strokes of impasto so well defined and so effective gives an insight into the creative process. This oil painting was purchased by the present owner direct from the artist’s studio in 1968.

title: Snow at Youlgrave
subject: Landscape
blurb: Knighton-Hammond adapted his paint-handling to the specific scene and weather conditions. Here he has painted a scene of Youlgrave under a blanket of snow in the winter of 1905 when he moved there from London and settled in the village. The buildings in the Derbyshire vernacular style are emblematic in the snow-covered landscape. The stone walls defined the road and field boundaries breaking up the areas rendered in colours of white and pale greyish blues. Paint at the depicted road surface is thicker than elsewhere in the painting and impasto is suggestive of the feel of disturbed snow. The lone figure walking in the road towards the spectator gives a sense of movement to an otherwise hushed composition in newly fallen snow. Aerial perspective is cleverly achieved to give depth using chromatic virtuosity with a restricted palette with subtle gradation of tones. This oil painting was purchased by the present owner direct from the artist’s studio in 1968. The painting must have meant a lot to Knighton-Hammond to have retained in his studio for more than 60 years!

title: Portrait of a Gentleman
subject: Portrait
blurb: The sitter appears to be deep in thought as he poses for his portrait. All of Knighton-Hammond’s portraits have individuality and this is no exception. He was beloved for his ability to capture the inner mood and personality of his sitter, who he would have painted from life. Using his penetrating powers of observation, he is able to convey human presence rather than artistic process. The modelling of the head and hand are exceptional and highlight the richness of the complexion. One is aware how much thought and technical knowledge have been brought to bear on this portrait. There is nothing laboured or heavy in the radiance of his flesh colours. Whilst the sitter appears to be in deep contemplation one is conscious that there was probably much dialogue taking place between the gentleman and the artist. The slight exaggerations in the hand makes for greater expression. This oil painting was purchased by the present owner direct from the artist’s studio in 1968.

title: Sunflowers
subject: Flower Study
blurb: This stunning study of sunflowers one feels is a focus on the artist’s own personal sensation and him seeking ways to translate this experience into paint. In conjunction with this variety of brushstrokes and texture of paint, Knighton-Hammond adopts a greater intensity in his colours as can be seen in the strength of the yellow, blue and green. It is closely descriptive of observed nature depicted in texture and chromatics – rich in form and vitality. Knighton-Hammond had the gift of capturing and transforming his motifs: he meticulously reproduced what he observed, and freely interpreted it, moving beyond the mere descriptive to create the pictorial equivalent of sensation. This oil painting was purchased by the present owner direct from the artist’s studio in 1968.

title: Youlgrave Church
subject: Streetscape
blurb: The view of Youlgrave Church from Church Street was painted in 1906 soon after the artist returned from London. The church and the typical Derbyshire vernacular architecture of the houses are well depicted. A shepherd is driving his flock of sheep along the street gives movement. It is a very social scene with children playing with a hoop on the pavement and other figures outside the church yard and outside their house. There is a feeling of engagement by the artist – a sense of touch in the composition and a focus on interaction. This oil painting was purchased by the present owner direct from the artist’s studio in 1968.

title: Ditchling Beacon
subject: Landscape
blurb: This landscape has an instinctive feeling for light, colour and tone which enabled the artist to produce works of luminosity, clarity and space. The watercolour focuses on the overall effect of the scene rather than details within it. The inward depth and spaciousness draw the spectator firstly observing the foreground pond, the masonry wall, gate and trees. The elements of the composition are formed with a profusion of constructive brush strokes yet when the picture is viewed from a distance there is a perfect blend giving an unerring sense of total effect.

title: Moreton Old Hall, Cheshire
subject: Landscape
blurb: This iconic Tudor Manor House dates from the 15th century and is famed for being rather ‘wonky’. This is the result of historic settlement in the foundations due to the marshy ground on which it sits. The building is of timber framed construction with a heavy gritstone slab roof covering. Knighton-Hammond shows us the construction features and chose to depict the south porch and Porter’s Lodge in this etching. The adjacent bridge over the moat has a lone figure looking over the parapet giving a sense of scale as do the ducks at the water’s edge. This etching is beautifully crafted with skill and sure knowledge of what the etching plate was going to produce when the print run was made. The detailing of the architectural features demonstrates Knighton-Hammond’s virtuosity of his draughtsmanship early in his career.

title: Penniless Porch, Wells Cathedrals
subject: Cityscape
blurb: From early in his career, at first sight this watercolour has a very limited palette. None of the usual slashes of red. The artist is, however, simply painting what was before him. Located in the Market Square, Penniless Porch is an entrance to the Cathedral Close and the Cathedral beyond. This is the manmade world of masonry and paving almost devoid of nature. The scattered figures do add a touch of colour as well as scale and movement. Without being slavish to detail, the architectural elements demonstrate the period of history from when the historic buildings were built. There is a grey sky but there is sufficient light cast to highlight the facades of the buildings.

title: Trees with Town Beyond
subject: Landscape
blurb: This view of a town, possibly Menton, through a vista in the trees shows what an instinctive feeling Knighton-Hammond had for light, colour and tone with watercolour. This enabled him to produce a work of luminosity and clarity. The richness of the greens and browns in the foreground are so fresh and immediate. The silhouette of the town in the background is very atmospheric and conveys space and depth to the composition. The hazy sky strikes shadows which add to and enriches the colour effects.

title: Cattle in a Landscape with a Rainbow
subject: Landscape
blurb: This landscape with grazing cattle captures the immediacy of the sensations created by nature. The watercolour exploits its special ability to convey light and space. Executed on the spot the composition possesses great freshness, colour and atmosphere. The dominant tree is rich in colour and form. The cattle have been rapidly drawn with the brush with direct watercolour creating movement and spontaneity. Knighton-Hammond uses the sky to dramatic effect – the light across the landscape and the arcing shaft of light on the right which surely will soon become a colourful rainbow.

title: The Ditchling Postman
subject: Portrait
blurb: Joseph Faulkner was the Ditchling Postman and was to sit for his portrait for the artist on a number of occasions always wearing his uniform. The head is painted using thick impasto oil paint modelling the volume and giving a richness to the complexion. All of Knighton-Hammond’s portrait have individuality and Joe is no exception. Even though the sitter appears slightly stiff in his pose, one can imagine there was dialogue taking place between sitter and artist. Knighton-Hammond has captured a good likeness of Joe, which was essential as everyone knew this popular local man and as was the portrayal of his character. Knighton-Hammond conveys human presence rather than mere artistic process important though that was. The slight exaggerations in the hands makes for greater expression. The background is relatively simple but works to project the sitter forward into the space of the spectator.

title: Iris, the Artist's Third Wife
subject: Portrait
blurb: This charcoal portrait sketch of Iris reminds me of the words of one of our greatest art historians, Sir John Pope-Hennessy, ‘One of the mysteries of drawing is that the greatest artists can achieve a sense of volume through line alone’ (JP-H, Raphael, p41). This drawing is a means of giving expression to his feelings for his wife. Iris’s head is drawn with a deceptive simplicity and very few lines convey volume. We know he has captured her likeness from other paintings and photographs. There is great delicacy and control on show here in this sketch which also captures the inner mood and personality of his sitter. The portrait is given greater prominence by the dark shading to the background. From the inscription the portrait appears to have been carried out in the couple’s caravan in 1938.

title: Cattle in a Landscape
subject: Landscape
blurb: Knighton-Hammond was always happy to be out painting in the fields of local farms. He knew the farm owners well, most of them featured in his paintings. He was, therefore, always welcome on their land and his presence caused them amusement and pleasure. The cattle here, some standing and grazing and the others lying down, are painted with spirited brush strokes – quick and vibrant. There is a power and energy in the structuring of the animals. The eye of the spectator is lead into the picture from the foreground grass which is rich in harmonious modulation. The background trees are in a blue/green atmospheric colour. The sky is grey but still gives luminosity to the composition.

title: John, the Artist's Son
subject: Conversation Piece
blurb: This is a quick watercolour sketch of the artist’s son, John sitting on the grass. There is an instinctive feeling of light and colour. The artistic expression was clearly influenced by his feelings for his boy and he captures his character and we know it was a good likeness. One is immediately aware that dialogue is taking place between the sitter and the artist and that in turn is transferred between sitter and spectator. There are a few traces of charcoal in the outline of the figure but the majority is pure watercolour applied with the brush at speed. The vigorous figure drawing with its stress on anatomical detail sits comfortably as a balance composition as the background projects John into the space of the spectator. This is not easy on a flat piece of paper but that illusion is the skill of the artist with effortless ease and gracefulness. There is a great charm in the gentle radiance of John’s fresh colours and in the soft atmosphere which envelops his figure.

title: The Fireplace
subject: Interior Scene
blurb: Knighton-Hammond focuses on the inglenook fireplace probably in his home in either Misterton or Seaborough. Within the fireplace recess are the fire dogs which support the logs and the intricate cast iron fire back. To the side of the fireplace is part of a smoker’s chair. This everyday household feature has been cleverly elevated into an art form. Knighton-Hammond could see artistic beauty and amply compositional strength in some quite mundane subjects and brings them to life in a very colourful way. With this watercolour, Knighton-Hammond’s aim was for simplicity and directness of statement, which the medium is particularly adept.

title: Market in Menton
subject: Streetscape
blurb: Knighton-Hammond clearly enjoyed being out and about in the market in Menton. The people in the town must have been used to seeing the English artist with his paintbox in the streets and market squares. Here, he captures the people going about their shopping and chatting to each other. The figures are painted with quick, spirited brush strokes giving movement and spontaneity. The facades of the imposing buildings are bathed in hazy sunlight. The trees in the square give verticality to the composition and one can almost feel the texture of the bark on the trunks.

title: Flower Market in Menton
subject: Streetscape
blurb: Whatever clues to artistic procedure Knighton-Hammond had managed to glean for himself in the South of France and in Italy between 1922 to 1932, the tuition that he received at Manchester Municipal School of Art under Adolphe Valette gave him a firm sense of direction. On the Continent, he quickly gained an understanding of the dynamics of urban life in France and Italy. His emerging mastery of architectural squares painted in an Impressionist style is evident here in the Flower Market in Menton. Amid a profusion of constructive brush strokes, executed on the spot, the work possesses great colour, light and immediacy giving the painterly illusion of movement and spontaneity. With the clusters of figures engaged in everyday conversation, one is aware a human story is being told in each part of the square. Knighton-Hammond captures the intimacy and the hustle and bustle of the market encapsulated by the architecture which is painted with great freedom and accuracy without being slavish to detail. The market stall and figures are produced with the brush. He blends his tints on the paper while wet and with such knowledge as to achieve great fluidity and gets everything just right compositionally.

title: Hill Top Town, Franco/Italian Riviera Region
blurb: The composition of this watercolour draws the spectator from the foreground to the hill top town proudly perched on the rocky outcrop. The trees in the foreground are rich in colour and form. The arched bridge appears to be part of the access road network up to the town. The church is the only defined building with the rest rendered as impressions but achieves what the artist intended. Knighton-Hammond captures the geography of the area and focuses on the scintillating sunshine spread across the landscape. The artist has presented the town from a dramatic viewpoint giving a sense of his own excitement as he discovered the beauties of the setting.

title: Derbyshire Dales
subject: Landscape
blurb: This watercolour of the Derbyshire Dales would date from around 1905. The river is probably the Lathkil. There is a three arched bridge spanning the river in the distance. Cattle are grazing at the river bank. The watercolour has been applied very fluidly. The foliage is rich in colour and form.

title: Montacute Priory
subject: Landscape
blurb: This unfinished work gives us an insight into Knighton-Hammond’s technique with painting in watercolours. With the brush and a stick of charcoal he outlines the main features of the composition. The building on the left in the Gatehouse to the Priory at Monacute House and on the right is the Church of St Catherine. Moving objects such as the ducks would have been quickly sketched in. The static features such as the architecture and the trees were given structure and detail. The sky would have followed. Knighton-Hammond would normally work en plein air.
