Here the sky appears bleak so it may well have been the artist was rained off. He put the picture in his portfolio and never got around to completely it in the studio. The painting would probably date from 1945 when we know Knighton-Hammond painted another painting of the Priory.

title: Haystacks
subject: Landscape
blurb: This watercolour by Knighton-Hammond is reminiscent of Claude Monet’s Haystacks, with not only the subject but also with the depiction of light, colour and mood. Again, like Monet, he has taken a seemingly mundane and uninteresting subject and managed to create something so beautiful and expressive. For the Impressionists, including Knighton-Hammond, light was the principal agent and the source of light and its ever-changing effects was the sky. Knighton-Hammond recognised its importance and never treated it as merely a background as it was paramount for adding drama and atmosphere. For this close descriptive of observed nature, he uses colour to describe not only direct but also reflected light. Painting en plein air with an instinctive feeling, Knighton-Hammond used unblended colours from his paint box applying them at speed, with extraordinary gusto, in broad, flourishing strokes with supreme confidence. This vitality of brushwork and the colour and light gives movement to the composition. Every stroke of the brush, seemingly so careless, has been evidently well thought out, and the artist’s sure hand enabled him to indicate form, colour and transparency with one energetic sweep of the brush producing luminosity and clarity. The foliage is very rich in colour and form and is the major element of the composition. Knighton-Hammond was a master at giving life to his works of art. The spatial organisation of this picture heightens the visual effect.

title: Anemones
subject: Flower Study
blurb: This study of a vase of anemones is full of colour and there is a disposition of space within the flower arrangement. As with all Knighton-Hammond’s flower studies the formality is broken by placing the odd flower on the table. He probably got into trouble as his third wife was a qualified flower arranger and would bring the display into the studio all immaculately presented. The artist used to remove and place a few blossoms adjacent to the vase to make it less formal! The colour washes to the background have the effect of projecting the flower display forward towards the spectator.

title: Near Sospel, 1928
subject: Landscape
blurb: The view of the Maritime Alps is flanked by two trees. With minimal colour and tonal changes, the artist manages to draw the spectator’s eye upwards to the mountain top village just visible through the atmospheric haze.

title: Near Courmayeur, 1923
subject: Landscape
blurb: Courmayeur is an Alpine resort at the foot of Mont Blanc in northwest Italy. The dramatic sky is allowing shafts of light to illuminate the iconic snow-covered mountain. This lighting effect almost appears that the mountain is admitting light rather than just reflecting it. Knighton-Hammond uses the most unlikely colours in the mid-foreground but to very good, atmospheric affect.

title: The Terrace Steps, Haddon Hall
subject: Landscape
blurb: This watercolour of The Terrace Steps looking towards the Hall would date from around the late 1890s or early 1900s. The south east elevation of this impressive, historic building is extensively covered in foliage. Knighton-Hammond cleverly uses different brushwork to give textures to the different foliage of the grass, hedge, plants and trees in watercolour. The steps with the masonry balustrading shows skilful perspective along with the seat. The young artist was beginning to show maturity in the quality of his work.

title: Derbyshire Dales
subject: Landscape
blurb: There is an intensity of light in this oil painting resulting from a combination of colour, variety of brush stroke and texture of the thick impasto paint. There is a scintillating movement of sunshine across the landscape and the river cascading down the waterfall. The brush strokes evoke the shimmering light on the water. With daubs of paint the foliage is very rich in form and colour. Even early in his career, Knighton-Hammond was able to achieve a close descriptive of observed nature. This resulted in his study of light, of coloured shadows of the tree and atmospheric effects in the background hills. The time the artist spent in Youlgreave and the surrounding area was particularly important to his career development.

title: The Market in Menton
subject: Streetscape
blurb: This watercolour would have been undertaken soon after Knighton-Hammond moved to the Continent in 1922. He was drawn to architectural squares and French pleinairism and Impressionism. The artist had an instinctive feeling for light, colour and tone which enabled him to produce works of luminosity and clarity as can be observed in this watercolour. The buildings surrounding the market square are depicted with a stylistic freedom of touch without slavishly representing detail. The quickly applied brush stokes of the figures give a painterly illusion of movement and spontaneity.

title: Dawn on Mont Blanc from near the Val D’Aosta
subject: Landscape
blurb: This atmospheric watercolour has Mont Blanc silhouetted against the cloudless blue sky. It offered Knighton-Hammond the chance to explore the pictorial possibilities of a landscape void of human activity to optimise the aesthetic response to nature. The foreground colours are very fluid drawing the spectator’s eyes to the majesty of the mountain. This picture was exhibited at the Royal Glasgow Institute of Fine Arts in 1952.

title: Evening in Spring – Lathkil Dale, Derbyshire 1908
subject: Landscape
blurb: We know the time of day and season from the title of the picture and one feels this is the landscape just recovering from winter. The River Lathkil appears to originate near Monyash and runs through Youlgreave and Alport before it joins the River Wye. The river widens out at numerous places and there are various changes of levels creating stepped waterfalls. Knighton-Hammond chose both a stepped waterfall and widening out of the river to set up his easel and paints. The valley has a steep bank populated with trees which are reflected in the slow running water of the pool area. There appears to be a boathouse structure projecting out into the river from the bank. The foliage in the foreground is rich in colour and texture.

title: The Parson’s Orchard, Youlgreave, Derbyshire – Spring 1908
subject: Landscape
blurb: When Knighton-Hammond returned to the Midlands from London in 1905 he settled in Youlgreave. We know he had a love of the Derbyshire Dales and appears to be out painting from nature at every opportunity. The apple trees in the Parson’s Orchard are in full blossom and ducks waddling around giving movement to the composition. The dry-stone wall divides the foreground from the background. The cottages with their smoking chimneys are silhouetted against the background hills of the Peak District depicted in an atmospheric blue.

title: A Spring Morning, Middleton, Derbyshire 1908
subject: Landscape
blurb: This landscape is early in Knighton-Hammond’s career and shows his competency in oil paints. 1907 and 1908 were significant years for the artist as he had autumn scenes of Derbyshire accepted by the Royal Academy. Early in the spring of 1908 this picture, the quality of which would have been on par with the RA exhibits, was produced. In the foreground sheep are grazing in the orchard giving movement to the scene. The apple trees are in blossom adding to the colour. The cottages beyond the orchard are in the Derbyshire vernacular style and their subtle perspective adds to the visual impact regards to creating depth. The handling of the paint depicting light, shade, colour and atmosphere show a significant level of maturity and demonstrates a close descriptive of observed nature. There appears to be a direct relationship between the texture of the paint and the character of the landscape itself.

title: Extensive landscape with a tree
subject: Landscape
blurb: This extensive landscape is dominated by the large tree in the foreground. The decorative foliage is very rich in form and colour. Knighton-Hammond gives the picture depth through its successive horizontal planes from the band of light green grass and shadow of the tree in the foreground, the bright green grass band in local colour running into the deep blue atmospheric landscape beyond to the horizon where it meets the sky with its ever-changing moods. One can feel the movement of the sunshine across this landscape which adds to the strength of colour in Knighton-Hammond’s descriptive of observed nature.

title: A Street in Grimaldi
subject: Streetscape
blurb: This watercolour of a narrow street in Grimaldi, which is a town close to the France/Italian border, shows Knighton-Hammond working with a surprisingly restricted colour palette. The main focus are the figures going about their business ascending or descending the sloping street. These would have been painted at lightning speed to give movement and spontaneity to the composition. The building flanking the street is depicted in a very Impressionistic style – not being slavish to detail and that provided dissolves into the fabric of the façade. Even with a restricted palette Knighton-Hammond still creates a sense of light and space.

title: Evening, Grimaldi Church, 1926
subject: Streetscape
blurb: Knighton-Hammond inscribed this watercolour as ‘Evening, Grimaldi Church, 1926’ and it features the Chiesa dei Santi Angeli Custodi (Church of the Holy Guardian Angels) in the Piazza Angeli Custodi, Grimaldi di Ventimiglia. Bathed in sunlight, the figures give an idea of scale and movement to the composition. The architecture is depicted in an Impressionist style not being slavish to detail with much of it being dissolved into the facade. The spectator is aware of the conversations taking place between the figures. The artist was not able to get much distance away from the facade of the church in the piazza but he was able to depict the elevation of the church and the tower. He also shows the tunnel for the road which runs through part of the building.

title: Milking Time After a Wet Day
subject: Landscape
blurb: In his latter years Knighton-Hammond could often be found visiting local farms. He knew the farmers well and was always welcomed to set up his paints. In this watercolour the cattle are meandering around the farmyard waiting for the dairyman to guide them to the milking parlour. The figures amongst the cattle give scale and movement to the composition. The buildings at the edge of the farmyard give a degree of perspective. The cattle have been painting at speed and even with the foreshortened animals their solidity and stature has been skilfully achieved. The standing water in the farmyard present from the recent storm has been cleverly used for reflections adding to the overall colour scheme.

title: Hyde Park, London
subject: Landscape
blurb: This coaching scene in Hyde Park was probably painted soon after the artist moved from Nottingham to London in 1900. The coach being pulled by four horses is clearly on the move. The coachman and passengers riding on top of the coach are in their Edwardian finery. There is probably more passengers inside. There is a lone rider following the coach and a dog giving chase. Coaching, hunting and race meeting scenes were subjects the younger artist was producing to help pay his rent and get him through the tough times.

title: The Terrace Steps, Haddon Hall
subject: Landscape
blurb: The Terrace Steps at Haddon Hall would have been painted on a very early trip by the budding young artist, Arthur Hammond in the late 1890s. The grand external steps rise up from the Upper Lawn up to the balustraded Winter Garden. During his painting expeditions to Haddon Hall, Arthur was given tuition by local artists who were also working at the iconic stately home.

title: Plum Blossom Cottage, Woodford
subject: Landscape
blurb: Plum Blossom Cottage was at Woodford in Cheshire. The thatched cottage has plum trees in the garden hence the name. This is one of a number of watercolours undertaken from the garden of the cottage. The picture is freely painted with a good play on light and shade. The chickens in the foreground add to the interest.

title: Pines on Cap Martin
subject: Coastal Scene
blurb: Whilst living in Cap Martin, Knighton-Hammond used to be up and out in the early morning to capture the different light effects offered by the Mediterranean. In this watercolour he uses the pine trees, with their rich evergreen foliage, to frame the scene across the bay. The morning atmosphere baths the coastline in hazy sunlight with the architecture blending into the mountainous backdrop. This would have been painted by Knighton-Hammond at lightning speed in a free, Impressionistic manner.

title: Portrait of Iris Knighton-Hammond
subject: Portrait
blurb: This portrait is of Knighton-Hammond’s third wife, Iris. She is turned side on to the artist and looking over her left shoulder. The clever application of watercolour serves to create the modelling, light and shade and the facial features which gives the likeness. The sitter is looking intensely at her relatively new husband and has a look of contentment. As always Knighton-Hammond captures the inner mood and personality of the sitter.

title: Italian Roses
subject: Flower Study
blurb: With his box of pastels Knighton-Hammond worked rapidly to sketch these roses in reds, yellow and white with green foliage. There is some blending and some visible stokes of the pastel sticks to create the roses and leaves. The vase is possibly silver reflecting the colour of the table cloth. The dark background projects the flower study forward.

title: Flowers with vases
subject: Flower Study
blurb: It looks like Knighton-Hammond raided the house for vases and flowers to put this arrangement together. The vases are known to us from other flower studies. A good variety of flowers have been selected and, as always, some are laid on the table. The artist creates a good disposition of space with the arrangement. A very colourful display which was probably painted in the studio later in life.

title: Freda
subject: Portrait
blurb: A very quick red chalk drawing of Freda. The outline would have been quickly followed by the salient features of her face and hair. There is very little modelling to the head yet it conveys volume. Knighton-Hammond showed great delicacy and control with his chalk. Freda’s jacket is articulated with a blunter chalk and different applicational pressure gives a sense of volume in the body. Very few lines were used to represent Freda’s skirt but again it is draped over legs to good effect.

title: Mary and Her Mother on the Steps
subject: Conversation Piece
blurb: Another affectionate study of Mary and her mother. They are sitting on external steps with May part in sunshine and part in shadow. A very Impressionistic watercolour with the physical structure of the steps and balustrade painted with great freedom and without being slavish to detail.

title: Early Evening, Kensington High Street, London
subject: Streetscape
blurb: This oil painting of Kensington High Street in the muted early evening light makes it simply evident that the lessons of Impressionism had been absorbed fully by Knighton-Hammond. His skill in the handling of paint is everywhere apparent in this streetscape from the spirited brushstrokes of the architecture and the foliage of the trees. The representation of the scene from a dramatic viewpoint with panoramic structure powerfully engages the spectator’s interest. The daubs of thickly applied pigment and bold accents of evening light and shadow on the street and the figures suggesting movement and spontaneity give a feeling of life in the paint and in the painting. Whatever clues to artistic procedure Knighton-Hammond had managed to glean for himself in the South or France and in Italy have been brought to bear on this painting. However, the tuition that he received at Manchester Municipal School of Art under Adolphe Valette gave him a firm sense of direction. One is aware how much thought and technical knowledge have been brought to bear on this painting. The linear perspective and the brilliant rendition of the facades and roofs reveal a painter of considerable control and power. The overall composition makes this picture a true masterpiece arguably on par with any streetscape carried out by the French Impressionists.

title: Sailing Boats in Harbour
subject: Coastal Scene
blurb: The tide is out in the harbour and the exposed hulls of the beached sailing boasts are being inspected by the attendant figures. Others are looking on with interest. The size of the foreshortened sailing boat in the foreground can be gauged by the scale of the figures adjacent and the beached rowing boat toward its stern. The harbour appears busy with boats moored up. The water with the reflection of the white sail appears to be calm but with a slight shimmer. This is another good example of how Knighton-Hammond uses clean washes of colour to achieve the maximum luminosity. The technique, which he perfected, gives his watercolours a clear and distinctive style, evident in this accomplished composition.

title: Stormy Day, Wales
subject: Landscape
blurb: Knighton-Hammond has managed to capture rushing skies, changing moods and shifting light in this Welsh landscape. The rather subdued colours denoting the successive planes giving depth to the picture taking the spectator’s eye through to the rugged mountains in the background. There seems to be almost a direct relationship between the application of the paint and the character of the landscape itself.

title: The Albert Memorial, Kensington Gardens, London
subject: Landscape
blurb: The Albert Memorial in Kensington Gardens was built to commemorate the death of Prince Albert in 1861 to the design of Sir George Gilbert Scott. The monument in the Gothic Revival style is viewed from under a canopy of trees, is well into the background in Knighton-Hammond’s watercolour. The grass and tree foliage are portrayed in strong greens reverting to blue in the far background. The figures in the mid-foreground give a sense of scale and distance.

title: The Sisters
subject: Coastal Scene
blurb: The Sisters are Knighton-Hammond’s daughters Marjorie and Dorothy in Colwyn Bay in June 1912. The girls are at play on the beach. One feels a great deal of affection has gone into this watercolour with his daughters the centre of his attention.

title: A Venetian Canal
subject: Cityscape
blurb: This watercolour would have been painted soon after Knighton-Hammond arrived in Venice in 1922. Full of compositional details, the spectator in confronted by two pali di casada – stripped canal poles at the waterside. A pair of gondolas are moored up. The arched bridge spanning the canal have figures crossing. Clever brushstrokes evoke shimmering light reflecting off the water. Majestic Venetian architecture in the background is bathed in sunlight. There is some clever shading from the right.

title: Stormy Morning, Old Court, 1945
subject: Landscape
blurb: The landscape is limited to a silhouette against the stormy sky. Knighton-Hammond produced and experimented with many cloud studies. He appears to have enjoyed the rapid notation of an ever-changing cloud formation and working at speed would have suited his style. When in London he used to visit the Tate Gallery to study the collection of John Constable’s cloud studies. He was well aware of the importance the sky was to any composition.

title: A Street in Manchester
subject: Streetscape
blurb: This drawing is an example of the technical virtuosity of Knighton-Hammond’s draughtsmanship. Superb architectural detailing, fine linear perspective and he uses the amount of graphite on the paper to illustrate light and shadow. Even the lamp post add much to the composition. The busy figures and the horses and carts give a sense of scale and spontaneity.

title: Alport Mill, Derbyshire
subject: Landscape
blurb: This view of Alport Mill on the River Lathkill has been painted with considerable delicacy with thickly applied pigment and bold accents of light and shadow. The latter being cast on the building by the large tree precariously overhanging the river. The decorative foliage of the river banks and trees are rich in form and muted colour. One can almost feel the mist coming off the waterfall.

title: Cattle in a Landscape
subject: Landscape
blurb: This early landscape gives hints that Knighton-Hammond was moving towards a freer style. The spirited brushstrokes depicting the stone wall at the side of the track, hedge, fence, trees and cattle. The colours are subdued and one can assume he has not yet come under the influence of Adolphe Valette at Manchester Municipal School of Art. In the background the trees are silhouetted against a grey sky.

title: Flowers in a Glass Vase
subject: Flower Study
blurb: A profusion of flowers! The flowers in a glass vase blends into the flowery wall paper behind. Fortunately, the red, white and yellow blossoms stand out from the riot of colour in the background.

title: Cromford Court, Manchester, 1922
subject: Streetscape
blurb: This drawing on Cromford Court looking across Corporation Street to Bull’s Head Yard, Manchester was drawn in 1922. This is a master class in linear perspective and architectural detailing. The hatching cleverly shows the areas of shadow and light. The figures provide scale and movement. One has the feeling that this drawing was destined to be turned into an etching.

title: On the Farm
subject: Landscape
blurb: This is an attention-grabbing farm scene due to the fact it is so full of content. The reflective water in the foreground starts gently rhythmic division between land and sky – the flat planes of the pool, field, fence, cornfield, hedge and tree and the thatched house silhouetted against the ever-moving sky. This picture is engaging with everyday farm subjects with minimal human presence optimises the aesthetic response to nature.

title: Figures in a Park
subject: Conversation Piece
blurb: This freely painted multi-figural composition is exploiting watercolour for its special ability to convey light and space. One is very much aware that with every cluster of figures seated on the benches in each part of the composition, a human story is being told. A picturesque watercolour painted with effortless ease and gracefulness.

title: Margaritas
subject: Flower Study
blurb: This flower study is full of intense light and clarity. Knighton-Hammond enjoyed having flower arrangements in his studio, normally set up by his third wife and then dishevelled by the artist to lose the formality. The clusters of flowers clearly have a disposition of space within the arrangement. A very clever depiction of Margaritas.

title: Derbyshire Dales
subject: Landscape
blurb: This oil painting of the Derbyshire Dales shows how Knighton-Hammond can, in conjunction with this variety of brushstroke and texture of paint, adopt a greater intensity in his colours. He also uses brushstrokes to evoke the shimmering light reflecting off the water. The atmospheric blue background has a church tower silhouetted against the sky. The decorative foliage is rich in form and colour. The cattle give a sense of scale and movement to the composition.

title: Moonlight
subject: Landscape
blurb: This early oil painting, possibly of the Derbyshire Dales, is full of moodiness from the moonlit rural scene. There is an eery tranquillity created by the slow moving river. The cattle are grazing near the farm building. With the lighting there is limited gradation of tone to work with yet Knighton-Hammond cleverly achieves aerial perspective helped by the position of the trees.

title: Gypsy Encampment
subject: Landscape
blurb: This oil painting, thick in impasto, is rich in colour giving a greater intensity of light. The caravans give perspective and the horses facing the spectator show clever foreshortening. The texture of the paint has been used for the grass bush, tree and the cloud study. There seems to be a direct relationship between the texture of the paint and the character of the landscape. The boy in the foreground brings a human touch. This painting demonstrates Knighton-Hammond’s compositional strength.

title: The Azo Shed, Dalton Works, Huddersfield, 1919
subject: Industrial Scene
blurb: This painting of the interior of the Azo Shed at the Dalton Works was undertaken whist Knighton-Hammond was engaged by the Government and British Dye Stuffs during World War I. His task was to illustrate the buildings and processes being built and undertaken as part of the war effort. He remained with British Dye Stuffs for a short time after the war had ended. The interior is full of perspective – the structure steelwork of the building, the diminishing size of the vats and the walkway all take linear forms. The figures going about their work give a sense of scale. The colour scheme was restricted to what lay before him.

title: Cattle on Bale's Farm, Misterton
subject: Landscape
blurb: The clump of trees synonymous with Druids Hill, Bale‘s Farm, Misterton are portrayed in the background. The cattle are just meandering with the one on the right appearing to look inquisitively at the artist at work. The bold watercolour would have been painted late in Knighton-Hammond’s career. The brushwork is rapid and more attacking in execution.

title: The Fall and Expulsion from the Garden of Eden
subject: Conversation Piece
blurb: This drawing was made from the fresco by Michelangelo Buonarroti in the Sistine Chapel in the Vatican. The drawing is dated 1911 so it would have been done from an image rather than the actual fresco. The composition tells the story – on the left are the fallen pair, on the right the pair expelled from Paradise. In the centre the anthropomorphised tree of knowledge with the female tempter. The drawing was exhibited at the Royal Watercolour Society Galleries in 1956.

title: Chickens in a Landscape
subject: Landscape
blurb: This watercolour has depth through it successive planes – foreground field, hedge row with trees and gate, fields beyond painted in atmospheric blue and the sky – a moody cloud study. The chickens are happily pecking away in the foreground and add colour and movement to the composition. With this picture Knighton-Hammond is responding to nature presented to him in this landscape.

title: Broad Street, Ludlow
subject: Streetscape
blurb: Knighton-Hammond set himself up in Broad Street to undertake this detailed architectural study. The building at the head of Broad Street is the Butter Cross. This historic street has a range of buildings from different periods from medieval timber framed structures to the Butter Cross with its classical features. St Lawrence’s Church tower stands proudly above the streetscape. The figures and vehicle bring life and a sense of scale. The composition demonstrates the technical virtuosity of his draughtsmanship.

title: Cap Martin
subject: Landscape
blurb: This is a very moody landscape of Cap Martin in the South of France. The artist has kept his watercolours very fluid and has created a misty atmosphere. Knighton-Hammond has been very restrained with colour which indicates he paints what is before him in nature rather than what he wants to see.

title: Portrait of Sir Frank Brangwyn
subject: Portrait
blurb: Knighton-Hammond produced a red chalk drawing of Brangwyn from which to produce this etching. One can only imagine the conversation taking place between these two seasoned artists when this was going on. The portrait would have been carried by Knighton-Hammond in the mid to late 1930s when he was living in Ditchling. Sir Frank also lived there and the two were close friends. The original red chalk drawing and a copy of the etching are in The National Portrait Gallery, London. If one goes onto their website to view the drawing you will see that in transferring the drawing to his etching plate Knighton-Hammond has not lost any of the speed of line or spontaneity. This is a real character study with personality present in the etching. The slight exaggeration in the hands give greater expression. One feels that this is two artists expressing their friendship.

title: Mary and her Mother reading a book at Porto Maurizio
subject: Landscape
blurb: Mary and her mother are sitting reading a book at Porto Maurizio in Italy. The clear blue sky made for a sunny day. The dominant tree is in blossom. The wall and arched gateway are bathed in sunlight. The Knighton-Hammond family were frequent visitors to Monte Calvario, Porto Maurizio to visit their architect friend Edgar Wood during the late 1920s and early 30s. Mary and her mother frequently featured in the artist’s compositions.

title: Mary and her Mother at Monte Calvario
subject: Landscape
blurb: Mary and her mother are sitting on the hillside at Monte Calvario, Porto Maurizio in Italy. The Old Monastery behind the figures was the rented home of Knighton-Hammond’s architect friend Edgar Wood (1860-1935). The architecture feels monumental and is cleverly detailed. The trees, rich in foliage, contrast with the blue Mediterranean sky. Edgar Wood stayed at the Old Monastery whilst he designed and built his own arts and craft house a short distance away. The Knighton-Hammond family were frequent visitors to Monte Calvario and it is likely that Edgar, an accomplished artist, encouraged Knighton-Hammond to paint in pastel. Mary and her Mother frequently featured in the artist’s compositions. His young wife was the love of his life as was his daughter.

title: Sheep in a Landscape
subject: Landscape
blurb: This watercolour was carried out early in Knighton-Hammond’s career and shows an excitement for the natural phenomena. Painted methodically it represented what was before him in the landscape. The elements are painted in a very correct manner as his style was developing. Within a decade or so he would be under the influence of Adolphe Valette which brought about significant development for his future career.

title: A Grey Day - Mermaid Street, Rye
subject: Streetscape
blurb: The Mermaid Inn is on the right in shadow on what Knighton-Hammond’s tells us by inscription was a grey day. The very famous street scene does have some sunshine breaking through further down the hill. He has depicted the architecture in a very Impressionistic manner and has not been slavish to detail. The colourful figures give a sense of scale and movement to the composition.

title: View of the Dolomites
subject: Landscape
blurb: This pastel explores a panoramic structure and minimal narrative. Knighton-Hammond boldly describes the mountains with quick strokes of the pastel stick giving form using the pastel as it comes – no blending or blurring of the lines. The ever-changing clouds have been described with rapid notation blending and softening the pastel with his fingers. The composition is light and bright and is an accomplished exercise in the art of pastel painting.

title: Continental Market Stall
subject: Streetscape
blurb: This busy market is full of hustle and bustle and were seen by Knighton-Hammond to be celebrations of urban life. The buildings surrounding the market have been atmospherically depicted with colour wash with little attention to detail. Instead, the artist has concentrated on the spontaneity of the figures outlined in watercolour at lightning speed and later filled in with the relevant colour which he would have made a note of. A bright, colourful scene showing Knighton-Hammond at his Impressionistic best.

title: Venetian Lagoon
subject: Coastal Scene
blurb: In conjunction with his variety of brushstrokes and texture of paint, Knighton-Hammond adopts a greater intensity in his light and colours when painting in Venice. This oil painting of boats in the lagoon is exceedingly rich in colour and full of vitality. Merchandise is being loaded or unloaded by the busy figures who give life and movement to the composition.

title: A Passing Storm
subject: Landscape
blurb: The extensive landscape was carried out later in Knighton-Hammond’s career and is full of variety – rushing skies, changing moods and shifting light. As Knighton-Hammond enters upon the last phase of his career it was not a period of decline but on the contrary, the one which marks the culmination of his greatness as an artist. Here we see freedom of handling and richness of atmosphere. There is standing water in the foreground and some foliage with extensive fields beyond in which cattle are grazing. A farmstead stands on the horizon at the intersection with an extensive sky all to good effect.

title: Portrait of Shirley Hyatt
subject: Portrait
blurb: This portrait of Shirley is painted with pure, direct watercolour with no under drawing. This takes supreme confidence painting in this way with no pencil guidance. The sitter appears confident posing as this was one of a number of portraits of her by Knighton-Hammond so she was happy doing so. The artist has used the paper to play a part in the colour scheme for the portrait. A few contour brushstrokes make up Shirley’s upper body and outfit cleverly conveying volume. The head is brilliantly painted and captures the sitter’s inner mood and personality. As always with Knighton-Hammond, there is a feeling of moisture in both eyes and lips. When viewed from a distance one does not realise how much blue has gone into the build up of the portrait. The artist has stressed the anatomical detail with his vigorous brushwork and achieves a carefully balanced composition.

title: Portrait of John, the Artist's Son
subject: Portrait
blurb: This portrait of John, the artist’s son sitting in his highchair is striking for the expression of the sitter and the colourful clothes he is wearing. John is captured with rosy red cheeks and a shock of light brown hair. His outfit is a vibrant yellow. His eyes, staring out at the spectator are big and striking. One can see the moisture in both eyes and lips. All elements are painted with thick, impasto oil paints giving texture and assisting with the modelling. The light-coloured background projects John out of the picture plane into the space of the spectator.

title: Still Life with Flowers
subject: Still Life
blurb: This colourful, striking still life is vibrant. The two blue vases contain red and pink roses with green foliage. Knighton-Hammond’s third wife was a trained flower arranger and took control when it came to setting up the flower studies. Much to her annoyance, the artist did not like formality so he would remove a few of the blossoms and place them haphazardly on the table adjacent to the vases. It used to get him in trouble! There is a feeling of real space around the flowers. On the wall behind there is a head of a classical or mythological figure.

title: The Harbour, San Remo
subject: Coastal Scene
blurb: This watercolour of the harbour at San Remo would have been painted soon after Knighton-Hammond arrived on the Continent in 1922. All the lessons learnt from Adolphe Valette in Manchester are on display. The Impressionist approach to light, colour and tone using watercolour and exploiting its special ability to convey freshness and immediacy. The sailing boat at anchor in the centre of the composition has been boldly painted. The buildings of Old Town San Remo are bathed in sunlight and depicted in a very free manner. The cathedral - Concattedrale di San Siro, San Remo – is silhouetted against the mountain range in the background.

title: The Picnic
subject: Landscape
blurb: This extensive landscape and cloud study features two young figures by a small, smoky fire where they were having their picnic. The rapid notation of the ever-changing clouds creates a changing mood. There appears to be a source of light through the clouds at the horizon. The picture has depth through successive planes building up the landscape. The large tree has dense, dark foliage. The loan figure in the mid-ground would have been part of the picnic party.

title: Barges on the Thames
subject: Boating Scene
blurb: This pastel of the Thames was painted on a sheet of sandpaper – Knighton-Hammond must have run out of pastel paper so had to improvise! He uses strong colours for the elements in shadow. The bow of the sailing boat is depicted in a strong orange and is cleverly reflected in the shimmering water. He creates a slight mistiness of atmosphere by skilful blending of pastel with delicacy and control. The composition is well drawn as we would expect with the technical virtuosity of Knighton-Hammond’s draughtsmanship.

title: The Masseuse, Burgess Hill, 1938
subject: Conversation Piece
blurb: This very quick charcoal sketch was undertaken at Burgess Hill in 1938 whilst Knighton-Hammond was living at Ditchling. The person receiving the massage is created with very little contour lines and minimal hatching. The masseuse receives more attention and charcoal. Simple outline and heavy hatching create solidity and form giving a sense of effort being applied in the massage. A convincing drawing with quick execution.

title: Landscape with Grazing Cattle
subject: Landscape
blurb: Knighton-Hammond selected a view between two trees to set himself up to paint this pastel landscape. The leafless trees have spindly branches so do not obscure the landscape and sky beyond. The grazing cattle in the foreground set-off the transitions of horizontal planes – cattle, trees, fields, hills and sky. The small sticks of pastel were ideally suited to rapidly notate the elements before him. He uses strong colours to portray the light in this panoramic scene and conjures up an atmosphere created by the soft pastels evoking the brightness of the day.

title: Threshing Time
subject: Landscape
blurb: Throughout his long career, Knighton-Hammond’s choice of subjects and the ways in which he treated them went through many striking changes. When he was living in Somerset and Dorset it was the local farms that interested him. The everyday subjects and collective activity taking place in nature greatly appealed to him. There is a lot going on in Threshing Time. There is a multitude of figures at work or play in, on and around the farm vehicle. Children are at play on the hayrick. Corn has been bagged up awaiting transportation. The artist’s Impressionistic approach is a direct response of what is before him. The watercolour was rapidly executed, focusing on the overall effect of the scene rather than details within it. His instinctive feeling for light, colour and tone enabled him to produce works of great freshness and immediacy.

title: Boat Yard, Conwy Bay, North Wales
subject: Coastal Scene
blurb: This early oil painting of the boat yard in Conwy Bay portrays a rather dull day. Knighton-Hammond uses a profusion of constructive brushstrokes in this composition. He uses impasto with visible brushwork to evoke the shimmering light of the water and to give texture. Conwy Castle is silhouetted against the sky. The two figures at the water’s edge give a sense of scale and movement.

title: A Market Square in Verona
subject: Streetscape
blurb: This market square in Verona was painted with speed, freedom and accuracy and is remarkable for its apparent naturalism – its linear perspective, the brilliant rendition of the stuccoed walls and the architectural detailing of the campanile, windows and Juliette balconies all painted in an Impressionist manner. There are accents of light and shadow on the street. With the figures engaged in conversation the artist takes every life and elevates it into an art form.

title: Ditchling 1935
subject: Landscape
blurb: This watercolour is a triumph of fluidity as the artist captures the immediacy nature before him. Working in the open air, Knighton-Hammond applies colour washes at speed with an instinctive feeling for light and colour creating maximum luminosity and clarity. From the reflective pond in the foreground, Knighton-Hammond uses horizontal planes to give depth depicted by the bank of the pond, field and tress beyond and ultimately to the sky.

title: Tree in a Landscape
subject: Landscape
blurb: This landscape in pastels suits and explores the light and colours of nature. Working rapidly with his box of pastels, Knighton-Hammond was able to fix the scene and then manipulate the gradular softness improving textures and transitions of hue of nature before him. He could blur the edge of the moving cloud with his finger tips or add streaks of light as the illumination changed. The artist used narrow, flat planes to give depth from the foreground with the fields and hills creating a gently rhythmic division between land and sky. The dominant tree looks a little precarious with its apparent lean.

title: Park Lane, London 1929
subject: Streetscape
blurb: Knighton-Hammond enhanced this pencil drawing by adding watercolour to the foliage of the trees in the foreground. Executed in 1929 Park Lane was by then a very desirable place to live and work. The façades of the buildings would have been sketched at speed clearly depicting the different styles and eras of architecture. Building works were taking place behind the buildings evidenced by the two cranes towering above the roof tops.

title: Covered wagon and sheep, Jeffrey’s Farm, Misterton
subject: Landscape
blurb: Farmer Jeffrey is attending his sheep beside a covered and an open wagon. The composition is built up with a considerable amount of brushwork. Each stroke of the brush, which seems to attack the paper so casually is in fact carefully and masterfully executed. Knighton-Hammond uses form, colour and light to give life to the work of art which is one of the necessary tasks of the true artist. This demonstrated the compositional strength of the painting with man and nature in harmony. Later in life, Knighton-Hammond’s choice of subjects and the ways in which he treated them went through many striking changes to which this picture is testament.

title: Drying the Sails, Venice
subject: Boating Scene
blurb: This colourful watercolour depicts and busy Venetian canal with sailing and rowing boats and figures engaging in everyday subjects and activities of this iconic city. There is a slight heat haze with the facing façades of the buildings in sunlight and the façade following the canal running away from the spectator in shade. The water reflects the colours of the sailing boats with brushwork evoking the shimmering light. The scene offered Knighton-Hammond an opportunity to explore the pictorial possibilities of striking atmospheric effects that impose an overall unity onto the composition.

title: Arundel Castle
subject: Landscape
blurb: Arundel Castle was built at the end of the 11th century by Roger de Montgomery, Earl of Arundel. This is a bold watercolour with regards to form and painted on a dull day when the artist had returned to England from the French Riviera. He clearly managed to restrain himself and adapted his colour palette to suit the light and colour of Arundel. Knighton-Hammond set himself up north west of the castle and focuses on the circular Keep on the left and Bevis Tower on the right.

title: Evening Light - Cathedral, Dieppe
subject: Streetscape
blurb: This evening scene is dominated by the façade of the cathedral with the evening light highlighting the stonework. In the foreground, in subdued light, the market stalls are still busy and in each cluster of figures a human story is being told. Painted quickly with the brush it gives the painterly illusion of movement and spontaneity. One can see Knighton-Hammond’s emerging mastery of urban streetscape painting in an Impressionist style and clearly there is a deepening understanding of the dynamics of urban life in France. It is likely that Knighton-Hammond was on one of his many trips across the channel when he stopped off at Dieppe to paint this picture.

title: Portrait study of a woman
subject: Portrait
blurb: In this red chalk drawing the sitter has her head turned to the right and is in profile. Knighton-Hammond captures the profile in light outline for the face and goes in heavier with the chalk for the hair and blouse. The key elements – eye, nose and mouth are drawn to perfection. With delicacy and control the head is modelled with effortless ease and gracefulness capturing the inner mood and personality of the sitter.

title: Chateau de Polignac, Cervennes, France
subject: Landscape
blurb: The impressive Forteresse de Polignac presides over the village of Polignac and the Velay plateau on the outskirts of the medieval town of Puy en Velay. Painted en plein air, Knighton-Hammond was a natural painter, skilful, energetic and varied which is everywhere apparent in this watercolour. From the spirited brushstrokes of the buildings, trees and landscape to the majestic fortress silhouetted against the skyline. The artist was well versed in exploiting the special qualities of watercolour to convey light and space.

title: North End Farm, Ditchling
subject: Landscape
blurb: North End Farm is bathed in sunlight and shadow and the artist exploits the special ability of watercolour to convey light and space. The figures give a sense of scale and movement to the composition. The three-dimensional pictorial space is created by the diminishing scale of the line of fence posts. In the Impressionist manner the shadows are not just an absence of light, but light of a different quality and value.

title: Caesar's Tower, Warwick Castle
subject: Landscape
blurb: Caesar’s Tower, Warwick Castle was painted when Knighton-Hammond was on holiday from the war work he was engaged in at British Dyes in Manchester and Huddersfield. The artist had clearly mastered the art of depicting architecture. There is a variety of buildings from different eras and status but dominated by the 14th century Caesar’s Tower. The freedom of the watercolour, combined with elements of charcoal drawing, shows the development in the artist’s style and technique following the influential time he spent studying under Adolphe Valette at Manchester Municipal School of Art. It was quite rare for Knighton-Hammond to use charcoal or any form of drawing in his watercolours. The charcoal elements do add to the composition particularly in the leafless tree with its spindly branches allowing a view of the castle beyond.

title: Study of Hands
blurb: This study of hands in red chalk was carried out in October 1938 when Knighton-Hammond was staying at Moynes Court, Cheptow. This was the home of Brigadier General Edmund Herbert (1866-1946) who Knighton-Hammond met at his first Continental exhibition in San Remo in 1922. Knighton-Hammond’s drawing practice was speedy and economical in development. Hands are notoriously difficult to draw but here the artist has achieved realism using accuracy in outline, contours and hatching for light and shadow. There is subtle exaggeration with which the artist creates feeling of strength and vitality.

title: A Sussex Labourer
subject: Portrait
blurb: ‘One of the mysteries of drawing is that the greatest artists can achieve a sense of volume through line alone’ Sir John Pope-Hennessy; Raphael, 1970, p41. This quotation by one of our greatest art historians admirably sums up this red chalk drawing of A Sussex Labourer by Knighton-Hammond. He is able to impart a sense of volume and there is vibrancy in the lines; the thickness of which is created by minutely lessening or increasing the pressure applied thus lightening or darkening these lines. There is a crisp outline and deftly controlled shading in the modelling. The portrait is more than just skilful drawing and he was renowned for his ability to capture the inner mood and personality of his sitter, who he drew from life. Knighton-Hammond also shows great skill in depicting the hands which demonstrate strength by his subtle exaggeration and boldness in form.

title: Middleton Dale, Derbyshire
subject: Landscape
blurb: This early oil painting of Middleton Dale dates from 1907. The Autumn scene has a meandering waterfall at its heart. The artist uses the local colour of green for the foliage in the foreground and as the picture recedes into the hills in the background this changes, due to the vail of atmosphere, to blue achieve convincing aerial perspective. Arthur Hammond uses thick impasto paint to give texture and naturalism to his composition.

title: All Saints' Church, Evesham
subject: Landscape
blurb: This early oil painting of the entrance porch of All saints’ Church, Evesham would date from the early 1900s. The artist enjoyed depicting architecture from early in his career and there is a maturity in his grasp of linear perspective. He uses daubs of thickly applied pigment with accents of light and shadow to convincingly portray the historic building and the trees beyond to engage the spectator’s interest in the composition.

title: Villefranche-sur-Mer
subject: Cityscape
blurb: This watercolour in pale, fresh hues, has the imposing church of Eglise Saint-Michel de Villefranche-sur-Mer silhouetted against a cloudless sky. The emblematic architecture demonstrates Knighton-Hammond’s virtuosity with his draughtsmanship. Painted in direct watercolour, with no under drawing, with great freedom yet great accuracy with regards to linear perspective. The artist has not been slavish representing detail instead relying on the Impressionist approach which is completely convincing. The sea reflects his instinctive feeling for light, colour and tone bringing luminosity and clarity to the composition.

title: Emmeline Mary Knighton Hammond
subject: Portrait
blurb: This portrait in watercolour is of Emmeline Mary (May) Knighton Hammond, the artist’s second wife. They met when the artist was in hospital in San Remo where she was a nurse in 1924. This portrait would have been painted soon after they met. He has portrayed the sitter with great sensitivity and brings out her vulnerability. Fashionable for the 1920s, May has a bob haircut and with big brown eyes she tentatively looks out at the spectator with a hint of shyness.

title: The Gypsy Encampment
subject: Landscape
blurb: Knighton-Hammond creates a striking pictorial space for the gypsy encampment. Full of atmosphere achieved by quickly applied brush strokes giving the painterly illusion of movement and spontaneity, most significantly in the smoke rising from the camp fire. The gypsy woman in the foreground is exceedingly rich in colour and full of vitality with the obvious and visible brush strokes. Knighton-Hammond has refrained as much as possible from mixing colours on his palette and applied them pure in daubs thickly applied with bold accents to evoke the transience of light.

title: Coastal Scene
subject: Coastal Scene
blurb: This coastal scene, possibly on the Riviera, has an air of tranquillity about it. A lone figure in red sitting in quiet contemplation. The scene is dominated by a majestic tree colourfully depicted with foliage in a variety of shades of green. The shadow being cast is typically Impressionistic. Knighton-Hammond has executed this composition on the spot and he has exploited his ability in watercolours to convey light and space in his clear distinctive style.

title: The Rear Garden of The Bull, Ditchling
subject: Landscape
blurb: The clean washes of colour applied by Knighton-Hammond achieve great luminosity in the sunlit façade of the buildings viewed in Rear Garden of The Bull. One can observe the spirited brushstrokes of the foliage and the varying styles of architecture. The figures give the composition life and, painted directly and confidently in watercolour, one can appreciate the technical virtuosity of Knighton-Hammond’s draughtsmanship. The timber framed building is on the opposite side of the High Street and the building to the right is the rear of a house adjacent to The Bull.

title: Vieux Pont de Sospel
subject: Landscape
blurb: The Vieux Pont (also commonly known as Roman Bridge) is in the picturesque town of Sospel in the Maritime Alps was a favourite location for the artist. The double arched bridge spans the River Bévéra and was painted many times. Knighton-Hammond, painting en plein air, would have set up his paints in the riverbed to capture this emblematic structure with great freshness and immediacy. Knighton-Hammond’s instinctive feeling for light, colour and tone enabled him to produce works of luminosity and clarity.

title: The Avenue of Trees
subject: Landscape
blurb: The Avenue of Trees was in the grounds of Knighton-Hammond’s home at Old Court, Misterton, Somerset. The rows of plane and lime trees form an avenue of perspective which John, the artist’s son is wandering through. Sadly, the picture as faded over the years but still gives a powerful sense of Knighton-Hammond’s undoubted ability with watercolours and landscapes.

title: Mary and her mother sitting on Edgar Wood's seat
subject: Conversation Piece
blurb: Mary and her mother sitting on Edgar Wood’s seat at Monte Calvario, Porto Maurizio, Italy. The Knighton-Hammond family were frequent visitors to their architect friend Edgar Wood. The seat was designed by him and was located in his garden. Knighton-Hammond depicts this monumental work of art with all its architectural features and motifs in watercolour with great freedom yet great accuracy. Daughter Mary is being affectionately cuddled by her mother. The two often featured in the artist’s compositions during the late 1920s and early 30s.

title: Portrait of a Man
subject: Portrait
blurb: Knighton-Hammond’s portraits have individuality. He was renowned for his ability to capture the inner mood and personality of his sitter, whom he painted from life. This portrait of a man conveys sensitivity in the eyes and thoughtful expression such are the penetrating powers of observation of the artist. The complexion and the volume of the head is modelled with thick impasto oil paint. The articulated clothing gives solidarity and bulk of the anatomy. The simple background cleverly projects the sitter into the space of the spectator.

title: Albenga, Italy
subject: Streetscape
blurb: This street, Via Bernardo Ricci in Albenga, Italy is painted directly with the brush – no pencil under drawing. It is a busy picture with figures in clusters deep in conversation as they go about their activities. The buildings are finely depicted and from a photograph taken close to the spot where Knighton-Hammond had set up his watercolours, one can see the accuracy of the lines of perspective and the architectural details. An example of the technical virtuosity of his draughtsmanship and how the artist translates a scene into a convincing pictorial space with his watercolours. The precision of the brushwork heightens the visual effect. Knighton-Hammond captures the entrance to Santa Maria in Fontibus in the right foreground with the Cathedral di San Michele Arcangelo beyond the square with its campanile. As with many of Knighton-Hammond’s Continental pictures from the 1920s and early 30s, in this street scene in Albenga one can see the emerging mastery of urban streetscape painting in an Impressionist style with an understanding of the dynamics of urban life in Italy. Helped by the blue sky and bright sunlight, the artist here has an instinctive feeling for light, colour and tone enabling him to produce this watercolour of luminosity and clarity.

title: A French Fishing Port, Dieppe
subject: Coastal Scene
blurb: The harbour at Dieppe would have been painted on one of Knighton-Hammond’s many trips across the channel during the 1920s and early 30s. The imposing architecture of the buildings surrounding the harbour side are bathed in sunlight. The composition is busy with lively, spontaneous figures engaged in conversations on both the harbour and the boats in the water. The figures are all painted with direct watercolours with no under drawing. This is a sign of great confidence and skill.

title: Reeves the Tramp with a broken finger
subject: Portrait
blurb: The portrait of Reeves the Tramp with a broken finger completely conveys the human presence and character of the sitter rather than just artistic process – good though that is. Mr Reeves was probably passing through Ditchling and was invited into the studio like many locals, but each sitter had unique individuality. K-H appears to have been drawn to these characters who were both source material and inspiration for him. We know from a watercolour and etchings of Mr Reeves that the artist has captured a good likeness. The portrait demonstrates a thorough understanding of anatomy. The features are painted with supreme confidence: the eyes are striking conveying the character of the sitter; the complexions show the ruggedness which comes with hard outdoor work in all winds and weathers. There is a similar ruggedness conveyed by Mr Reeves’s heavy clothes.

title: Mrs Knighton Hammond
subject: Portrait
blurb: This pastel of Emmeline (May) Knighton-Hammond demonstrates how talented the artist was with the chalks. The articulated drapery received much attention in this portrait and the striking colours are kept fresh with pure direct pastel. The hair is cleverly depicted with texture and tonal highlights. The colourful clothing is exemplary as is the wallpaper in the background and one feels the sitter is projected into the space of the spectator – there is a definite disposition of space between the background and the sitter. K-H’s penetrating powers of observation were perhaps made easier with this portrait of his beloved wife. He goes beyond the merely physical to achieve a psychological likeness, communicating the soul and tenderness of the sitter conveyed particularly by her eyes and expression.

title: The Oak Tree, Shropshire
subject: Landscape
blurb: The Oak Tree is dominant in a Shropshire landscape. The use of watercolour is less transparent than we normally expect from Knighton-Hammond. There is a strength and depth in the colour palette and the range and tones used to give depth to the composition. The two figures walking into the landscape towards the gate create movement.

title: The Smithy, Woodford, Cheshire 1912
subject: Interior Scene
blurb: The interior of The Smithy at Woodford represents the technical virtuosity of Knighton-Hammond’s draughtsmanship. All the intricate details of the building fabric, equipment, materials and tools would have been painstakingly described with the etching needle into the wax on the etching plate. The open door and window allow light in and creates light and shade which the artist cleverly depicts with the amount of hatching and thus the ink left in the plate. This is an exercise in linear form description using line alone. One can feel the atmosphere of this workshop and its functionality and clearly shows the artist’s skill as an etcher.

title: Studies for Reeves the Tramp
subject: Portrait
blurb: This etching of the standing figure of Reeves the Tramp is complimented by a further study of his head and hand. This is Knighton-Hammond thinking and exploring on his etching plate. Drawn with fine draughtsmanship and the spontaneity has been transferred from drawing to etching plate. All the studies have solidity and volume created by skilful handling of the etching needle. The artist has used pastel to add colour to the composition.

title: In the Park
subject: Conversation Piece
blurb: This freely painted watercolour depicts a busy park with figures sitting on benches spread around a circular grass area. On each bench there are personal stories being told. The trees cast shadows on the gravel paths and lawn. The figures, whilst seated, still provide movement and spontaneity to the composition.

title: The Distressed Tree
subject: Landscape
blurb: This bold watercolour is dominated by the tree which is clearly in a distressed state. The broken bows have fallen to the ground adjacent making for an interesting composition not lost on the artist. The branches, littering the foreground, have been skilfully described with foreshortening and perspective. The trees in the distance have been rendered blending the wet tints of Autumn. The combination of cloud and sky makes for an interesting study.

title: The Man with a Scythe
subject: Portrait
blurb: The Man with a Scythe is Walt Eglon, a character from the Misterton area of Somerset. Freely painted in watercolour, the seated figure with the handle of the scythe over his shoulder. The face, partially in shade afforded by the brim of his hat, shows an amusing expression. This is likely the result of the relationship between artist and sitter. Knighton-Hammond enjoyed painting local characters. The soles of the hobnail boots are skilfully described. The country gentleman has all the signs of strength and ruggedness sitting on the grass which he will shortly be cutting.

title: Reeves the Tramp
subject: Portrait
blurb: This striking watercolour portrait of Reeves the Tramp was executed with a very limited colour palette. Reeves was a character who was known to Knighton-Hammond when he was living in Ditchling and featured in a number of works. The artist was renowned for his ability to capture the inner mood and personality of his sitter, who he always painted from life. The light is coming from the spectator’s left and the head is modelled on the light side with very few linear brushstrokes. This is an example of where skilful artists can convey a sense of volume through line alone. The greater amount of work is on the shadow side. The right hand is skilfully rendered showing the strength and ruggedness of the sitter. The background would have been boldly carried out at speed yet the sitter appears to be projected forward into the space of the spectator.

title: Piazza della Signoria, Florence
subject: Streetscape
blurb: This watercolour would have been painted on one of Knighton-Hammond’s early visits to Florence in 1922. The artist set himself up with his watercolours inside the Loggia dei Lanzi in the Piazza della Signoria looking towards the Palazzo Vecchio. Michelangelo’s David (a copy with the original the star exhibit in the Galleria dell'Accademia) stands majestically outside the seat of government. Cellini’s Perseus with the Head of Medusa stands proudly looking into this iconic square. There is a powerful sense of authority about this freely painted picture. Like many of Knighton-Hammond’s Continental pictures of this period one can see the emerging mastery of urban streetscape painting in an Impressionist style and an understanding of the dynamics of urban life in Italy. Helped by the bright sunshine, Knighton-Hammond here has an instinctive feeling for light, colour and tone enabling him to produce this watercolour of luminosity and clarity.

title: Plum Blossom Cottage, Woodford
subject: Landscape
blurb: Plum Blossom Cottage is in Woodford, Cheshire. It featured in many paintings carried out by Knighton-Hammond between 1910 and 1920. A bright, colourful composition bathed in sunlight. The whitewashed thatched cottage sets the scene enhanced by the plum blossom and other foliage. The attendant chickens give a sense of movement in the foreground.

title: The Butter Cross, Ludlow
subject: Streetscape
blurb: This watercolour of Ludlow features the corner of the Butter Cross looking toward the top of Broad Street. Knighton-Hammond painted and etched a number of views in and around Broad Street in this historic Shropshire town when he visited in 1919. The architecture is well depicted in a free manner not slavishly representing detail. The freedom and confidence of the brushwork would have come from the time the artist studied under Adolphe Valette at Manchester Municipal School of Art in the years before the Great War. The beauty of Ludlow, and Broad Street in particular, is the varying periods of history and architecture. The artist confidently handles timber frame, masonry and brick structures achieving remarkable naturalism. Executed on the spot, the composition possesses great freshness and immediacy.

title: A Wet Square in Venice
subject: Streetscape
blurb: This watercolour of Venice was carried out soon after Knighton-Hammond arrived in the city in 1922. The dominant structure is the Loggetta del Sansovino designed by Jacopo Sansovino (1486-1570) and completed in 1546. It forms the base of the Campanile in St Mark’s Square. It is clearly evident that the artist was in his element in the depiction of the Venetian architecture with his interpretive brushwork. The characteristic composition methods of the verticality of the Loggetta and the linear perspective of the Biblioteca Nazionale Marciana beyond shows that nothing was so powerfully emblematic as Classical architecture. The library was also designed by Sansovino and is a masterpiece of Renaissance Venice and faces the Doge’s Palace across the piazzetta. Knighton-Hammond’s freer more Impressionist style does not slavishly represent detail, it does, however, ooze spontaneity and inventiveness demonstrating his competence in its mastery. The figures and reflections from the wet paving give movement to the composition.

title: Portrait of a Woman
subject: Portrait
blurb: Knighton-Hammond captured the thoughtful gaze of the sitter. He was renowned for his ability to capture the inner mood and personality of his sitters, who he painted from life. Here, with the light source coming from the spectator’s right, the artist uses light to convey the volume of the head with tonal modelling. The texture of the oil paint adds to the complexion. Knighton-Hammond’s portraits have individuality and the plain, dark background of this work projects the sitter into the space of the spectator.

title: Cattle in a Farmyard
subject: Landscape
blurb: This farmyard scene portrays the elevated yard with cattle milling around. The buildings are described with good perspective and are freely drawn directly with the brush. Similarly, the cattle have great movement. The masonry walls are depicted without being slavish to detail. The dark clouds are contrasted by the ray of sunshine highlighting the yard.

title: Autumn in Wales
subject: Landscape
blurb: This watercolour entitled Autumn in Wales was exhibited at the Royal Institute of Painters in Water Colours in 1966. The artist has captured an atmospheric scene. The valley is bathed in bright sunlight in the distance with a storm closing in from the foreground. An impressive cloud study of contrasting weather. The clarity of light in the valley, which Wales is able to celebrate, is well defined using Autumn tints. One can imagine the impact this picture would have had on the walls of the Royal Institute of Painters in Water Colours.

title: Gladioli
subject: Still Life
blurb: This oil painting contains two images of the artist. The portrait bust is of Knighton-Hammond modelled in clay by Francis Doyle-Jones and was exhibited at the Royal Academy in 1926. The artist can also be observed working at his easel in the reflection in the mirror. The gladioli are colourful and well depicted. The items on the table – bust, flower pot and skull show good distribution of space and perspective. This painting is on the reverse of another painting – 25 pounder under a chestnut tree.

title: 25 pounder under a chestnut tree
subject: Landscape
blurb: 25 pounder under a chestnut tree portrays the artillery who were billeted at Knighton-Hammond’s home, Old Court, Misterton during the Second World War. The 25 pounder, a British field gun, under the tree was one of a number used by the army for training in the grounds. Another gun can be seen in the mid-foreground. To describe the elements of the composition, Knighton-Hammond uses daubs of thickly applied pigment and bold accents of light and shadow. The sunny day called for a bright, light palette. It demonstrates the artist’s command of the Impressionist style with an instinctive feeling for light, colour and tone enabling him to produce a work of luminosity and clarity. The soldiers give life and movement to the composition and the artist’s son, John, is showing interest watching the soldiers going about their duties. The oil painting demonstrates Knighton-Hammond’s considerable artistic skill and documentary accuracy. Painted in August 1942, St Leonard’s Church is visible in the background.

title: San Giorgio Maggiore, Venice
subject: Cityscape
blurb: When Knighton-Hammond was living in Venice he had a large output of works. San Giorgio Maggiore was a subject that appealed to him. Designed by Andrea Palladio, perhaps the most imitated architect or all time, Knighton-Hammond captures the view across the Giudecca canal. The emblematic architecture has been painted at speed with pure, direct watercolour. The perspective is a testament to the artist’s skill as a draughtsman. The complex of buildings is silhouetted against a deep blue sky. The gondolier in the foreground gives a sense of movement to the composition.

title: Landscape and Cloud Study
subject: Landscape
blurb: This landscape has a low horizon with the background foliage depicted in dark greens and atmospheric blue. The artist’s prime interest was the sky. The ever changing cloud formation would have been rapidly noted down in watercolour.

title: Haddon Hall
subject: Landscape
blurb: This pencil drawing of the Entrance to Banqueting Hall at Haddon Hall demonstrates the artist's skill with draughtsmanship when it comes to depicting architecture. The linear perspective is accurate, the foliage convincing and the hatching informs us of where the sunlight was coming from.

title: Pont Neuf, Paris
subject: Streetscape
blurb: This etching of the Pont Neuf over the Seine in Paris shows the technical virtuosity of Knighton-Hammond’s draughtsmanship. There is documentary accuracy in the artist’s mastery of urban streetscapes and emblematic architecture. The hatching provides linear form description. The clusters of figures, which are deep in conversation, show human stories are being told.

title: Atmospheric landscape
subject: Landscape
blurb: This atmospheric landscape is shrouded in mist. In the foreground there are buildings and trees. In the mid-ground there appears to be a river with mountains beyond. The banding of the foreground, mid-ground, background and sky gives depth to the composition rather than relying on the conventional gradation of colour and tone.

title: Concarneau
subject: Boating Scene
blurb: This picture of the harbour at Concarneau is dominated by the three sailing boats. Through the sails there is a view of the hillside buildings. Something of a ‘symphony’ in blue this watercolour would have been painted at lightning speed with a limited palette.

title: Venetian Canal Scene
subject: Cityscape
blurb: There is a striking contrast with bright sunlight and shadow with this Venetian canal scene. The gondola on the narrow canal is in the area of shadow as it passes through the archway. The iconic architecture, whether in sunlight or shadow, is depicted in an Impressionist manner and the linear perspective gives depth to the narrow vista.

title: Mrs Knighton Hammond and Mary
subject: Family Gathering
blurb: This family conversation piece is of Mrs Knighton Hammond (second wife) and daughter Mary sitting at a table under an umbrella. Mrs K H appears to be busy sewing whilst Mary is looking bored as she had probably been told to sit still whilst the artist quickly produced this watercolour. There is a lot of content in the picture and K-H has skilfully depicted sunlight and shadow. The glazed terracotta pot and the perspective of the empty chair provide real foreground space and depth to the composition and the tree and umbrella adds colour.

title: John Knighton-Hammond
subject: Portrait
blurb: This portrait of John, the artist’s son, poses with light coming from his right which assists the artist with the modelling of the head in particular. The light also seems to be reflected off the eye’s moist surface. John here is a young man dressed in a three-piece suit, collar and tie for his portrait. He is looking directly at his father and appears to be projected out into the space of the spectator. Knighton-Hammond was renowned for his ability to capture the inner mood and personality of his sitters, which he painted from life. He conveys his son’s human presence rather than mere artist process.

title: Portrait of a woman
subject: Portrait
blurb: This portrait in oils is rich in texture. The sitter’s hair in particular has been picked out with highlights and lowlights in impasto. The sitter appears a little uncomfortable in her pose with her arms folded. There is an intense look on the woman’s face almost expressing a desire for the sitting process to be completed.

title: John the artist's son
subject: Portrait
blurb: Knighton-Hammond enjoyed painting portraits of his family. This portrait of John, the artist’s son, has been delicately painted in pastels. John is sitting on a cushion placed on a chair and is looking intensely at his father at work. Modelling in pastel has been skilfully carried out achieving a three-dimensional effect as John appears distance from the background.

title: November Morning
subject: Landscape
blurb: This extensive landscape painted on a crisp, misty November morning is full of atmosphere. The cattle and figures give colour, movement and scale to the composition. The trees in the background have been sketched in with the veil of mist reducing the visible distance of the picture. The watercolour would have been painted at speed by Knighton-Hammond.

title: Wayford Manor
subject: Landscape
blurb: This watercolour of Wayford Manor near Crewkerne shows Knighton-Hammond at his Impressionist best. Painted during the 1940s or 50s there is an instinctive feeling for light, colour and tone which enabled him to produce a work of such luminosity and clarity. Wayford Manor was then owned by Mrs Knighton-Hammond’s relatives. The arched loggia was an early twentieth-century extension to the historic building designed by garden designer/architect Harold Peto. The powerfully emblematic Somerset vernacular architecture of the building with its window surrounds, arches, label mouldings, copings and garden balustrade and steps demonstrate the artist’s skill in the brilliant rendition of sun-bathed masonry of the south elevation. The figure in the garden gives scale and movement and the flowers add colour to the composition which powerfully engages the viewer’s interest.

title: Cloud Study
subject: Cloud Study
blurb: In this Somerset landscape, Knighton-Hammond positioned himself with large trees front and centre. The field in the foreground is painted in green – the local colour which gradually progresses into blue – the atmospheric colour in the background. The graduation of colour creates the depth to the composition. The main focus of the artist’s attention would have been the clouds. The quick brushwork rapidly notates the formation and movement of the clouds against the blue sky.

title: A Continental Garden
subject: Landscape
blurb: This entrance way to a Continental Garden is colourful and freely painted in watercolours. The perspective of the path draws the eye through the metal arches to the pillars at the end of the path. A very Impressionistic scene with an instinctive feeling for light, colour and tone giving luminosity and conveys space.

title: The Hunt
subject: Hunting Scene
blurb: This hunting scene has the huntsmen and hound giving chase to their quarry. Dressed in their hunting pink, the huntsmen are at full gallop. The artist has used local and atmospheric colours to give depth to the composition.

title: Venice
subject: Cityscape
blurb: This canal scene in Venice is remarkable for the architecture with its linear perspective and the rendition of stucco buildings adding up to a good pictorial effect. He had a mastery of urban streetscape painted in his Impressionistic style. The boats in harbour would be transporting goods to the island. There are gondolas as one would expect on a Venetian canal. The figures give movement and scale to the composition.

title: The Finish of the Derby 1902
subject: Sporting Scene
blurb: The finish of the Derby 1902 has Rising Glass beaten by Ard Patrick. At the finishing post the horses are in full gallop. The spectators are looking on dressed for the occasion. It is likely that Knighton-Hammond would not have been present at Epsom for the Derby. This picture was probably painted the following day when the artist got the results from the newspapers.

title: An Italian Garden
subject: Landscape
blurb: An Italian Garden in Boccanegra, Ventimiglia depicts the architectural features of free-standing columns. The tree and glazed terracotta pot adds to the composition.

title: A Gathering on a Harbour
subject: Coastal Scene
blurb: This gathering on a harbour has the colourful figures in conversation. There are boats in the background. The shadows contrast with the sunlight on the ground. The trees add colour to the composition.

title: Beach scene
subject: Coastal Scene
blurb: This beach scene has figures in the sea and those on the beach looking at those in the water. Mary, the artist’s daughter, is present with ‘Teddy’. Knighton-Hammond had a way of using multi-figural compositions going about everyday life and cleverly elevating it into an art form. The figures have spontaneity and movement.

title: Mary and Teddy
subject: Conversation Piece
blurb: Here the artist has concentrated on depicting his daughter Mary sitting on a colourful rug accompanied by her Teddy looking on. He has included some foliage to add to the colour scheme.

title: Kairouan, Tunisia
subject: Streetscape
blurb: This entrance to a building in Kairouan in Tunisia would have been painted on a trip Knighton-Hammond made to north Africa in late 1922. Executed with a limited palette, the artist has depicted the architectural details of the buildings in a free, Impressionistic manner.

title: Coaching Scene
subject: Streetscape
blurb: The passing coach and horses are being watched by the huntsman and his hound. The passengers are dressed in their refinery. The streetscape architecture is well depicted providing perspective and depth to the composition.

title: A Street in Nevers, France
subject: Streetscape
blurb: Knighton-Hammond set himself up in the Rue de la Cathedrale in Nevers to execute this watercolour. The tower and the main body of the Cathedral St Cyr Ste Julitte is visible at the end of the street. The building with the turret is on the corner of Rue de la Cathedrale and Rue Albert Morlon. Without being slavish to detail, the architecture is skilfully depicted. The linear perspective shows off his draughtsmanship. The artist is working in near monochrome in this instance. The figures and the horse and cart provide spontaneity and scale to the composition. .

title: Roses
blurb: This vase of roses painted in pastel was exhibited at the Pastel Society (No. 51). The pastel has been delicately blended and modelled to give the roses a three-dimensional roundness. The colours are vibrant and luminous.

title: An Italian Village
blurb: This Italian village scene is dominated by the single arched bridge. The buildings beyond are at the foot of mountains. The figures appear to be doing washing in the waterway. Very much Knighton-Hammond developing his Impressionist style.

title: Hunting Scene
subject: Hunting Scene
