blurb: The focus of attention in this hunting scene is the huntswoman at full gallop as she jumping the fence. Painted in 1900, soon after Arthur Hammond arrived from Nottingham, this and similar hunting scenes were produced on the kitchen table during though times for the artist. Primarily fun pictures painted to pay the rent early in the artist’s career.

title: Madonna della Costa, San Remo
subject: Landscape
blurb: The foreground and the trees frame the view of the Madonna della Costa in Sam Remo. The church and adjacent buildings are painted in a very Impressionist manner. The atmospheric blue mountains in background give depth to the composition.

title: Adlington
subject: Landscape
blurb: This scene of Adlington in Lancashire is cleverly depicted with the spector’s eye being drawn down the lane to the brick building. The shepherd driving his sheep provides movement as does the horse and wagon. The vernacular buildings provide linear perspective. Painted soon after the Great War it shows the artist developing a more Impressionist style.

title: Derbyshire Dales
subject: Landscape
blurb: This valley with a stream is in the Derbyshire Dales. The extensive landscape has great depth achieved by the use of local colour – the greens of the foreground and the mountain’s background where the greens appear blue due to the effects of the atmosphere. The foliage is well depicted as are the buildings. The sheep provide movement and scale to the composition. Painted is 1907, the artist is beginning to show greater competence.

title: The Manor House, Stokesay Castle
subject: Landscape
blurb: The Manor House at Stokesay Castle is an example of how to depict emblematic architecture. The rendition of materials in which the buildings are constructed are brilliant well described in watercolour. The light palette shows the influence of the Impressionists. The lone figure gives a sense of scale.

title: Liguria
subject: Landscape
blurb: This pastel of Liguria is a riot of colour. There are figures in the foreground which give a sense of scale to the adjacent foliage. The application of pastel is varied. The sky has been blended probably with the artist using his finger to give subtle gradation. The foreground appears to be pure, direct pastel applied with short strokes. The trees are a combination of both techniques. The bands of subject matter give recession and thus depth to the composition.

title: Haddon Hall
subject: Landscape
blurb: This scene of Haddon Hall in Derbyshire has great depth initially achieved by the river in the foreground. The landscape draws the eye of the spectator up to the historic hall. The buildings in the left adds with linear perspective. The foliage is depicted in a variety of greens and browns. The figures and cattle at the field boundary wall gives a sense of scale and movement to the composition. The architectural details and the masonry of the medieval hall are well rendered in watercolour.

title: Compton Dundon
subject: Landscape
blurb: The extensive landscape in pastel goes from local colour of bright green through to the atmospheric blue set against the horizon. In the mid-foreground there is a cluster of trees with a substantial stone building adjacent. The cloud study in soft pastel makes for a moody picture.

title: Menton from Caravan
subject: Landscape
blurb: This view of Menton was painted from Caravan. Old Town Menton is visible through the trees. The trees dominate the composition and are well depicted. The foreground is bathed in sunlight and shadow. The Old Town is also bathed in sunlight and is silhouetted against the sky. Knighton-Hammond’s work by this stage is showing the influence of the French Impressionists.

title: The Village, Prestbury
subject: Streetscape
blurb: This view of ‘The Village’ Prestbury would have been painted just before or during the Great War. It may well have been painted during a study trip painting en plein air under the guidance of Adolphe Valette, Master at Manchester Municipal School of Art. The streetscape is skilfully depicted with the different styles of architecture and fine perspective. The figures in the street provide movement and scale to the composition. There are signs here of Valette’s influence with Impressionism. This picture was exhibited 8 - 27 October 1973 at the Knighton-Hammond Exhibition at Stockport Public Libraries

title: The Avenue of Trees
subject: Landscape
blurb: The Avenue of Trees was in the grounds of Old Court, Misterton, Somerset, Knighton-Hammond’s home from 1940 to 1954. The trees are plain and lime trees and the leaves have the tints of autumn. Cattle are grazing in the field and the lone seated figure would have been John, the artist’s son. This watercolour would have been painted at speed in a very free manner.

title: Old Court, Misterton
subject: Landscape
blurb: A view of Old Court, Misterton, Somerset, Knighton-Hammond’s home from 1940 to 1954. The artist set himself up at the end of an avenue of trees to paint this view of his house. This would have been a very freely painted watercolour executed at speed. The lone figure gives a sense of scale to the composition.

title: Four-In-Hand
subject: Sporting Scene
blurb: Knighton-Hammond enjoyed attending horse related events and competitions. On this occasion, near Guildford in 1933, he used his pastels to produce this busy, colourful composition, full of life and activity. The coaches and horses are getting the attention of the gathered crowd and the judges. There is no over blending of the pastels relying on optical mixing of the juxtaposed colours and also the artist is relying on the colour of the paper in the composition. There is a delicacy in the application of the pastel.

title: The Cornfield
subject: Landscape
blurb: The cornfield has been harvested and the stooks of corn stacked ready for gathering. This painting of an extensive landscape with buildings and trees silhouetted against the blue sky is in rich oil paint. The foreground cornstooks and the trees have been painted with thick impasto paint giving texture to the elements of the composition. The darker colours of the background and the atmospheric blue to the hills give depth to the composition.

title: Hunting Scene
subject: Hunting Scene
blurb: This hunting scene shows the hunt at full gallop in pursuit of their quarry. It is likely that this watercolour was painted on the artist’s kitchen table. These ‘pot boilers’ as Knighton-Hammond later referred to them were produced for sale in order to pay the rent. The early years of the twentieth century were not easy when it came to making a living.

title: Styal, Cheshire
subject: Streetscape
blurb: Knighton-Hammond positioned himself at a junction in the road to paint this picture of a thatched cottage which dominates the composition in Styal near Wilmslow in Cheshire. A road sign gives directions. The watercolour has been freely applied but accurately describes the vernacular architecture of the village. Figures by the doorway of the cottage gives a sense of scale. The foliage of the trees, hedges and grass are competently depicted by the artist. This picture was exhibited 8 - 27 October 1973 at the Knighton-Hammond Exhibition at Stockport Public Libraries

title: A summer still life with flowers and silverware upon a patterned cloth
subject: Still Life
blurb: A summer still life with flowers and silverware upon a patterned cloth demonstrates Knighton-Hammond at his best in this genre. The rich colours of the thick impasto oil paint provide texture to the elements of the composition. The table cloth provides the linear perspective and thus the depth creating a disposition of space. The flower painting shows Knighton-Hammond’s skill in the subject. The silver candle sticks and vase are cleverly depicted with highlights and reflections. The porcelain figurine is skilfully depicted. The dark background with the dark sculptured head provides the setting for the colourful elements of the foreground. This is one of Knighton-Hammond’s best still life pictures.

title: Flower Study
subject: Flower Study
blurb: Knighton-Hammond used thick, impasto oil paints to produce this majestic flower study. Every element of the arrangement has been clearly defined and depicted. Placed in a colourful vase, this crowded flower arrangement achieves disposition of space giving roundness and depth to the composition due to the skill of the artist. Knighton-Hammond did not like over formality hence the reason for some of the blossoms having been removed from the vase and haphazardly placed on the table. The impasto gives texture to the detailed foliage. Within the flower arrangement are dog roses,foxgloves, delphiniums, dahlias and cosmos.

title: Market Scene
subject: Streetscape
blurb: This market scene is dominated by the powerfully emblematic architecture. The church with its imposing tower and the adjacent historic building has naturalism created by linear perspective and the skilful rendition of masonry and brickwork – not in detail but Impressionistic but sufficient for the materials to be identified. The modern undercover market contrasts with the historic buildings. Not only does Knighton-Hammond achieve pictorial effect but also documentary accuracy. The activities of the market traders with carts, vehicles, horses and figures provide movement and spontaneity. Knighton-Hammond portrays every day life and cleverly elevates it into an art form.

title: The Cronies
subject: Portrait
blurb: ‘The Cronies’ was an affectionate title Knighton-Hammond gave to this oil painting. A painting that was to remain with him from when it was painted in 1937 for the remainder of his life and is still in the Hammond family to this day. Painted in Blewbury in Berkshire, the two old characters were the village carpenter and a farm labourer – just the sort of people Knighton-Hammond loved to paint. Wonderfully painted in thick impasto oil paint with the brushwork economically articulating contour and defines form. With these characters the artist has gone beyond the merely physical to achieve a psychological likeness, communicating the soul and character of these two gentlemen. This has been possible by the skill in the painting of the heads and hands. The light coloured, plain background projects the sitters into the space of the spectator. Deep in conversation, the suggested movement achieved by the artist gives one the feeling of visually eaves-dropping on the two gentlemen’s conversation. The still life elements were also well depicted.

title: The Old Church Tower, Upton on Severn
subject: Streetscape
blurb: The Old Church at Upton on Severn would have been painted shortly after the Great War when Knighton-Hammond was on a painting trip covering Worcestershire and the surrounding counties. The distinctive tower is a remnant of an eighteenth century replacement for a medieval church which was badly damaged during the Civil War Battle of Upton in 1651. Barrels have been placed on the side of the main road through the village. The technique adopted by the artist shows him on a move towards Impressionism. The freely flowing watercolour is handled to good effect and there is accuracy in the structure of the composition with regards to perspective in the street scene. The figures give scale and movement.

title: San Remo Market
subject: Streetscape
blurb: This busy market in San Remo depicts the figures and stalls in bold colours contrasting with the pale, sunbathed buildings forming the back drop and the pale blue sky. The architecture has the feeling of Impressionism – sufficient details for the spectator to read the Continental style. The figures have spontaneity and movement created by the artist with speedy watercolour brushwork.

title: Cattle on hill at Bale's Farm, Misterton
subject: Landscape
blurb: The cattle grazing here on the hilltop on Bale's Farm, Misterton with the Manor House in the background are depicted in bright, fresh watercolour. The artist chose a clear day and cleverly illustrates the atmospheric colours on the background give the picture depth. The large tree adds to the composition creating harmony between livestock and nature.

title: A stroll in the avenue of trees
subject: Landscape
blurb: The artist has captured these colourful figures strolling between the avenue of trees. Executed with great spontaneity giving the life and movement to the composition. The foliage in its many shades of green has been built up using dabs of watercolour.

title: Street Market
subject: Streetscape
blurb: These market stalls have been set up on a pavement possibly in Tunis which would date the watercolour to the latter part of 1922. The produce has been placed on the stalls and in baskets on boxes at the front on the roadside. The stalls have simple fabric canopy roofs. The traders are behind the stalls awaiting customers. The colourful produce gives a touch of vibrancy to the sunbathed scene. The shadows cast on the walls from the stalls are painted in a blue – a completely different colour to the walls in yellow. In the Impressionist style, shadows are depicted not in an absence of light giving a darker colour but colour of a different value. The artist has used watercolours to good effect with regards to the freshness and luminosity of the scene. The figures provide a human touch to the composition painted in a very free manner.

title: Cattle in a hilltop field, Misterton
subject: Landscape
blurb: This watercolour would have been Knighton-Hammond working at speed. The cattle are sketched very freely and are silhouetted against the blue sky. The composition is in the main a cloud study and is strong in light and colour and the watercolour gives luminosity. Even as Knighton-Hammond was getting older he would still be out and about painting in the open air with great enthusiasm.

title: The Peacock
subject: Landscape
blurb: This watercolour of The Peacock was painted at Haddon Hall. The Winter Garden terrace is featured and is partially picked out in dappled light as the sun shines through the trees which are rich in colour and form. The masonry balustrade along the terrace and the top of the stairs which lead down to the lawn of the Upper Garden are skilfully depicted giving depth to the picture with perspective. The peacock provides movement and additional colour to the composition. When one looks at the picture you are almost waiting for the squawk of the peacock such is the realism!

title: The Fisherman's Cottage
subject: Landscape
blurb: This early landscape painting of the Derbyshire Dales features the Fisherman’s Cottage. The lively meandering stream with its waterfalls is well executed and the cattle gives movement to the composition. The Fisherman’s Cottage has smoke rising from the chimney. The tree and foliage are rich in colour and texture. There is a ruggedness about the landscape which the artist has conveyed in the picture.

title: Bowl of Roses
subject: Flower Study
blurb: During the latter decades of Knighton-Hammond’s life he turned to still life and flower painting. This Bowl of Roses is painted in thick impasto oils giving texture to the flowers and foliage. The artist did not like the formality of neatly arranged flowers so he would often take out the odd stem and place it on the table next to the bowl on this occasion. One has the feeling that the paint was applied at speed. The bowl is built up with a few brushstrokes giving it roundness. The flowers are created with broken brushstrokes creating the necessary three-dimensional feel. There is disposition of space within the display. All-in-all a powerful composition which stands alone on the table, detached from the background.

title: Piazza della Signoria, Florence
subject: Cityscape
blurb: Knighton-Hammond would have taken great interest in the art and culture of Florence. This watercolour of the Piazza della Signoria includes the iconic statutes on the right starting with Hercules and Cacus by Baccio Bandinelli, David by Michelangelo and the Fountain of Neptune by Bartolomeo Ammannati all outside the Palazzo Vecchio. To the left is the Loggia dei Lanzi. The architecture of the piazza is depicted in a free yet accurate manner. The figures are busy going about their business creating movement, scale and interest for the spectator.

title: The Village, Prestbury
subject: Streetscape
blurb: A scene of The Village in Prestbury probably carried out when on a painting trip from Manchester Municipal School of Art c1911. The Art Master, Adolphe Valette would take his students out to the picturesque Cheshire village of Prestbury to paint outdoors very much in the way of the Impressionists. The cottages in street scene of The Village are well depicted giving an immediate appreciation of the architecture in the facades. The perspective draws the spectator’s eye down the street. The figures give scale and give a sense of movement.

title: Hunting Scene
subject: Hunting Scene
blurb: This early hunting scene has the Master of the Hunt about to be served his tipple before setting off. The riders are in their hunting pink. The hounds are running freely giving a sense of movement. From the tints of the trees the scene appears to be Autumn.

title: St Martin's in the Field
subject: Cityscape
blurb: St Martin’s in the Field is in the north-east corner of Trafalgar Square. The emblematic neoclassical architecture was to the design of James Gibbs. The white Portland stone façade has been painted in a very precise yet Impressionistic manner. The fountain gives the picture a vaporous atmosphere. The figures gathered nearby are in conversation and give movement and scale to the composition.

title: Venice
subject: Streetscape
blurb: From the watercolour signature we know this canal scene would have been painted soon after Knighton-Hammond arrived in Venice in 1922. The buildings and campanile would have been drawn in watercolour direct with the brush. The perspective is accurate and the figures in the foreground and on the bridge give spontaneity, movement and colour to the composition.

title: Alport Mill, Derbyshire
subject: Landscape
blurb: Alport Mill in Derbyshire is a very atmospheric early watercolour. The rugged masonry of the mill is well depicted and smoke emanating from the chimney gives a sense of movement along with the chicken in the foreground. The waterfall adds to the cleverly created vaporous atmosphere. The foliage of the plants and trees is rich in form and colour.

title: On the steps
subject: Family Gathering
blurb: Mary and her mother (Mrs Knighton Hammond) featured in many of Knighton-Hammond’s pictures. Here they are sitting on some steps in conversation. His wife and daughter were very dear to the artist and this comes through in the sensitivity of the work. Painted in a very Impressionistic manner – with freedom and the composition is colourful and full of light.

title: Boats at Menton
subject: Coastal Scene
blurb: The sailing boats in the harbour at Menton are painted in a very free and colourful manner. The rich blue sky is reflected in the sea water. The quickly drawn figures give a sense of scale and movement to the composition. The picture is busy with vertical lines of the masts and rigging. A fresh and luminous watercolour full of Impressionism.

title: The finish of the race
subject: Sporting Scene
blurb: Paintings of the finish of horse races for Arthur Hammond was a means of paying the rent. He would buy a newspaper and find out the placings of the race and would paint the picture on the kitchen table. Times were tough when the artist moved to London in 1900 and producing ‘pot boilers’ as he called them was a necessity. Here the horses at full gallop may not be anatomically correct but they are generating excitement in the stands.

title: A Study of Heads
subject: Portrait
blurb: An etched study of heads consisting of a self-portrait of the artist and his son, John. Knighton-Hammond would have sketched the studies directly into the waxed etching plate with his needle. He experiments with the direction of the light and shadow to model the heads. He demonstrates his confident draughtsmanship and achieves a good likeness with simple lines.

title: Mrs Knighton Hammond
subject: Portrait
blurb: This watercolour of Mrs Knighton Hammond would have been painted at speed. There is limited paint in the picture but sufficient for all the salient elements to be present to give his wife the sensitive and thoughtful character which we know she had from the artist’s diaries. There is sufficient detail to give a good likeness and the human presence is there for all to see. Simple brushstrokes give solidity to the figure.

title: The Market Place, San Remo
subject: Streetscape
blurb: The Market Place, San Remo is a busy picture – full of life and drama. The many figures are engrossed in conversation. They have been quickly drawn with the brush in pure, direct watercolour achieving great spontaneity and movement. Pictures which engage with everyday subjects and collective activity were Knighton-Hammond’s forte. Having dashed down the figures – the moving elements - he was able to spend more time painting the trees and buildings beyond the market place. The foreground appears unfinished but Knighton-Hammond knew when to stop and let the sketching speak for itself.

title: San Giorgio Maggiore, Venice
subject: Cityscape
blurb: San Giorgio Maggiore, Venice is perhaps the most famous church in the city. Designed by the famous architect Andrea Palladio – the most imitated architect of all time. When Knighton-Hammond was painting this view, it was a dull day and this is reflected in the subdued colours and tones. There is a vaporous atmosphere creating a haze. The artist chose a side-on view of the church. The architecture is well defined. The sailing boat in the foreground gives movement to the composition.

title: Church of San Matteo, Laigueglia
subject: Landscape
blurb: The Church of San Matteo in Laigueglia, Italy is superbly depicted in bright sunshine and part shadow. The church towers are silhouetted against the rich blue sky. The foreground foliage is in deep green from the shadow being cast by the adjacent tree. This picture is Knighton-Hammond at his Impressionistic best using light and colour. There is a luminosity and freshness to the work.

title: The Morning of the Derby
subject: Sporting Scene
blurb: The Morning of the Derby is a rare example of a print taken from an original watercolour by Arthur Hammond. Pictures of race meetings were popular subjects in the early 1900s. This work was reproduced and sold through C E Clifford & Co of Haymarket. A busy morning at Epsom with crowds dressed up for the occasion. There is a lively atmosphere as the horse drawn coach makes it way through the onlookers.

title: A Cheshire Pool, Bramhall
subject: Landscape
blurb: This early watercolour of a Cheshire Pool in Bramhall demonstrates the artist’s skill in handling foliage, water and sky. The pool is reflective and the foreground colours have a hint of Autumn. The trees frame the receding landscape. The cattle in the field give scale and movement to the composition.

title: Cleobury Mortimer
subject: Streetscape
blurb: This early watercolour of part of the main street running through Cleobury Mortimer is colourful and immediately carries the spectator down the road such is the perspective. The different styles of architecture are well depicted. One can almost feel the surface of the pavement. The figures and horse and cart give scale and movement to the composition and the atmospheric blue on the horizon further adds to the depth.

title: The Old Monastery, Monte Calvario
subject: Landscape
blurb: This picture features the Old Monastery at Monte Calvario, Porto Maurizio. It sits high up overlooking the Mediterranean coast in Liguria. For a while this was the home of the artist’s Manchester architect friend, Edgar Wood. The Knighton-Hammond family were frequent visitors during the later 1920s and early 30s. The watercolour is painted with great freedom in the style of the Impressionists. The light appears to be at the forefront of the artist’s mind. The shadows cast by the trees are not represented in the colour with an absence of light but colour of a different value – a feature of the Impressionists.

title: St Oswald's Church, Grasmere
subject: Landscape
blurb: St Oswald’s Church in Grasmere in the Lake District is situated on the banks of the River Rothay in the centre of the village. The watercolour is painted very precisely in tones not normally used by Knighton-Hammond but this was an early picture and his style and technique were still evolving. The foliage of the trees and river bank and reflections in the water are very fluid and there is a sense of luminosity in the composition. St Oswald’s Church is the final resting place of poet William Wordsworth.

title: Chepstow Castle
subject: Coastal Scene
blurb: Chepstow Castle is freely painted in watercolour. The castle is perched on top of the cliffs with the sheer faces of the rock rising out of the water. The atmospheric blue in the background is contrasted by the green foliage around the castle. The River Wye is quickly sketched with minimal brushstrokes.

title: A coach and horses
subject: Sporting Scene
blurb: An early coaching scene with coachmen and well-dressed passengers riding on the open top. The coach and its four horses may be coming to rest at an entrance to a fine house. A pair of masonry piers frame the entrance. There is a boy at the side of the road bending over to get sight of the horses. A peacock appears to be watching the coach. The architectural details are finely depicted. These types of coaching scenes were essential for the artist to make a living in the early 1900s.

title: Henley 1901
subject: Sporting Scene
blurb: This is an early Arthur Hammond watercolour from 1901 of Henley. The heavily laden coach with its four horses is moving towards the viewer giving movement to the picture. The onlookers are dressed in their finery ready for the regatta. The buildings forming the streetscape are well depicted with good perspective and architectural detail. The trees create a very atmospheric work for this famous annual event. Arthur had not long moved to the area from Arnold, Nottinghamshire and would have enjoyed the spectacle of visiting Henley during this time.

title: The Carpet Sellers
subject: Streetscape
blurb: When Knighton-Hammond moved to Italy in 1922 he was keen to travel around as much as possible seeking new subjects. From Sicily he made a trip across the Mediterranean Sea to Tunis. He was interested in the hustle and bustle of the street markets. One evening he set himself up to paint the ‘Carpet Sellers’. The shop was housed in an arched structure with light spilling out from the open frontage. The colourful carpets were on full view. The Arab sellers are at the entrance awaiting customers and were probably intrigued by the artist painting them. The lighting effects make for a very moody picture.

title: Trafalgar Square
subject: Cityscape
blurb: This atmospheric watercolour of Trafalgar Square, London, has all the main landmarks included – Nelson’s Column, St Martin-in-the-Field, The National Gallery and one of the pair of lion’s statues. The picture engages with everyday subjects and collective activity with elegant, strolling figures enjoying themselves in this iconic location. The figures, mingling with the vehicles going about their business, occupy an important part of the composition and are closely observed giving movement and scale. The picture is painted in an Impressionist manner but with a limited and subdued palette to good effect.

title: Margaritas
subject: Flower Study
blurb: The margaritas and other flowers in this study is an arrangement in a blue jug which features in many of Knighton-Hammond’s still life paintings. The artist did not like formal flower arrangements hence the reason for a few of the margaritas being placed on the table. There is good disposition of space within the composition. The flowers stand out against a simple, plain background.

title: A Family Gathering
subject: Family Gathering
blurb: A quickly sketched composition of a family gathering. Mrs Knighton-Hammond (third wife) may be the figure on the right with the nanny and children with a picnic basket. This watercolour would have been painted at lightning speed.

title: Derbyshire landscape
subject: Landscape
blurb: An early landscape by Arthur Hammond with a crisp local colour foreground broken up by the river running through the composition. The large tree demonstrates the artist’s skill in depicting nature. In the centre of the picture is an arched bridge spanning over the river with a church spire beyond. The hills in the background are in an atmospheric blue colour. The component planes in the landscape provide aerial perspective. The flat fields, trees and hills create a gently rhythmic division between land and sky.

title: Moustiers-Sainte-Marie, Provence
subject: Landscape
blurb: Moustiers-Sainte-Marie is a mountain village in Provence. Its picturesque nature would have inspired Knighton-Hammond to get out his watercolours and paint. The elevated village is painted in a very Impressionistic and atmospheric manner. The architecture and the arched bridge are painted with just sufficient detail to be fully appreciated. The low-lying foreground is dominated by trees. The landscape and trees in the foreground are typically Mediterranean cypresses and olives. The cypresses cleverly draws the spectator's eye up to the mountain top village.

title: Piazza di San Marco, Venice
subject: Streetscape
blurb: This watercolour of the Piazza di San Marco, Venice was painted soon after a rain shower. The sun has come out brightening up the façade of the iconic San Marco viewed through the arches. The figures are leaving the shelter of the arches and walking out into the square. The emblematic architecture is very Impressionistic, drawn very freely but in sufficient details for the elements to be read. The figures have colour and movement and there are some which are picked out in red, a trademark of the artist having an element of red in his pictures. The square is given luminosity with the artist’s use of light, colour and tone further enhanced by the reflections from the wet paving.

title: Logging
subject: Landscape
blurb: This Autumn landscape has tree branches in the foreground with a sawing horse ready to reduce them to logs. As the picture recedes beyond the large, dominant tree there are a multiplicity of planes making up the fields which are divided by a fence running across the picture plane. The row of trees adds further division and the distance is marked out with strong, atmospheric blue which contrasts with the pale blue sky. There are buildings to the left in the mid-ground area. This would have been a very speedy watercolour with Knighton-Hammond freely drawing directly with the brush.

title: The Barns
subject: Landscape
blurb: This farmstead consists of barns with a hill beyond. The artist would have used bold colour washes blending the elements of the composition together to achieve maximum luminosity. Freely drawn with the brush at speed, he uses a light palette of colours in this Impressionist landscape.

title: Portrait of Wilf Weaver
subject: Portrait
blurb: The gentleman in this portrait is Wilfie Weaver, a local Ditchling character who was well known for carrying out maintenance on the roads in and about the village. As with so many locals, Mr Weaver was invited into Knighton-Hammond’s studio at Dymocks Manor to sit for his portrait. The artist shows his penetrating powers of observation as he conveys the human presence of Mr Weaver in this character study rather than mere artistic process, important though that is and the artist had this in abundance. The sitter is portrayed staff in hand sitting in a Windsor chair out of doors with sky and landscape as the backdrop, however, the powerful depiction of Wilfie is such that he is projected out of the picture into the space of the spectator well away from the background. Thick, impasto paint is used to model the head and hands giving texture and solidness. The clothing convincingly has the human structure beneath. The ‘old boys’ of Ditchling had great appeal to Knighton-Hammond. One can only imagine the conversations that would have taken place during the sittings. Wilfie has an endearing expression on his face probably as a result.

title: St Mary's Church, South Perrott
subject: Streetscape
blurb: St Mary’s Church at South Perrott in Dorset near the Somerset border has an instinctive feeling for light, colour, tone and space resulting in a work of luminosity, freshness and clarity. The Dorset vernacular architecture of the cottage and the ecclesiastical architecture of the church are beautifully depicted with a master class in perspective accuracy drawn directly with the brush. The figure moving through the churchyard gateway gives scale and movement. A label verso in the artist’s hand dates the picture to June 1948. Painted en plain air Knighton-Hammond still enjoyed painting on the spot and would have rapidly produced this watercolour hence it’s spontaneity.

title: A Continental Market Square
subject: Streetscape
blurb: Knighton-Hammond was a natural painter, skilful, energetic, instinctive and varied. His skill in the handling of watercolour is everywhere apparent in this scene on the Franco/Italian riviera. One can observe the spirited brushstrokes of the tree, the architecture, the market stalls and the spontaneous definition of the figures mingling in the hustle and bustle of the busy market. The artist’s feeling for light, colour and tone enabled him to produce these Impressionist works of luminosity and clarity whilst the composition powerfully engages the spectator’s interest.

title: A Street scene with Church
subject: Streetscape
blurb: The emblematic power of architecture dominates this watercolour probably in the South of France. The low-lying town with the tall buildings flanking the street with figures going about their business. The use of colour, light and shadow creates luminosity. The Church tower is silhouetted against the sky with the mountains beyond. Knighton-Hammond exploits the special ability for watercolour to convey light and space particularly well in this narrow vista of the street. The clusters of figures give movement and a human touch to create a composition technically skilful and of interest to the viewer. From the style of his signature this picture would date to around 1922.

title: The Priory, Montacute
subject: Landscape
blurb: With Knighton-Hammond’s work nothing was so powerfully emblematic as architecture. The Priory at Montacute demonstrates this and his command of draughtsmanship. The historic building dominates the composition swiftly drawn with the brush with great freedom yet great accuracy. Painted on the spot, the watercolour possesses freshness and immediacy with an instinctive feeling for light, colour and tone.

title: Digne, France
subject: Streetscape
blurb: As with many of K-H’s continental watercolours themes are woven into this painting. One can appreciate the importance of the architectural focal point, in this case the façade of the tall buildings dominating the town square in Digne, the importance of the clusters of figures, and the fact that, in each part of the composition, a human story is being told. The facades of the buildings are in shade but painted such that they are not just lacking light in their original colour but are in colours of a different value – very typical of K-H’s Impressionist style when it came to shadow. Indeed, there is good interplay between light and shade in the picture. The figures are painted with great spontaneity and give movement to the composition. This picture clearly demonstrates the artist was a passionate follower and admirer of the Impressionist movement, probably thanks to the teaching of Adolphe Valette at Manchester Municipal School of Art. He was a late Impressionist applying its principles several years after its creation.

title: Haddon Hall
subject: Landscape
blurb: The young Arthur Hammond was a frequent visitor to Haddon Hall in his early teenage years to develop his artistic career. He would work alongside established local artists who took him under their wings giving him guidance and instruction. This skilful watercolour of the facade highlights the significance of this monumental historic building set against the finely painted flower beds. A light, bright composition with fresh colours would have been painted around 1910 when the artist’s technique was showing maturity. This is evident in the skilful detailing and perspective in the handling of the architecture.

title: A Street in Paris
subject: Streetscape
blurb: The street scene may possibly have been undertaken when Knighton-Hammond was en-route to the south of France as the inscription mentions the sketches were carried out in 1922. A busy street depicted in both sunshine and shadow. The figures give life and scale to the composition. As always with K-H the architecture is so well drawn with linear perspective and detail.

title: Haddon Hall
subject: Landscape
blurb: A picturesque Haddon Hall is one of a number of similar scenes from this vantage point carried out by Knighton-Hammond. The river, trees and bridge in the foreground lead the spectator into this spectacular medieval castle perched majestically on the hill. The sunshine picks out the elevations which are devoid of ink. The artist cleverly shades the remaining elevations and fenestration. An accomplished etching of a much loved location where the artist spent a good deal of time in the early part of his career.

title: Cattle in landscape
subject: Landscape
blurb: This early etching has two cattle grazing in a field with trees in the foreground. As the picture recedes the artist has used the hedges running across the picture plane to give aerial perspective running into the hills in the far background. The trees also provide diminishing scale. The etching plate has not been over worked giving the minimum ink to describe the scene.

title: Durham
subject: Landscape
blurb: The immediate focal point of this etching carried out in 1918 is the street scene and its fine perspective in the houses fronting the highway. A horse drawn wagon appears to be preparing to make its journey up the hill. Tall trees break up the picture plane with Durham Castle nestled between them high up on the hill. The clever perspective draws the eye to the horizon.

title: A Derbyshire Landscape
subject: Landscape
blurb: This etching is probably of a landscape in Derbyshire in about 1910. To create the three-dimensional pictural space the artist uses diminishing scale to give perspective to the composition. This can be observed in the trees as they run from foreground to background. He also uses the amount of ink in the plate to give recession – more etched lines in the foreground and less as the picture moves to the horizon.

title: A study of Margaret
subject: Portrait
blurb: This study of Margaret in red chalk has the artist working to pin down and develop a composition. He has sketched her laying on what is probably a beach towel and has carried out various studies of her head. This is capturing the artist’s first thoughts and reveals his intentions. One can gauge that K-H was wholly immersed in his art – simultaneously, spontaneous and inventive. It is not known if the sketch was later used to produce a painting.

title: A sketch of Mary
subject: Portrait
blurb: This crayon sketch principally of the artist’s daughter would have been carried out at lightning speed. Knighton-Hammond was able to do quick, hurried sketches with surety such was his skill and technical virtuosity in his draughtsmanship. With a few lines he is able to bring solidity and volume to both figures in the composition.

title: Italian coastal town
subject: Coastal Scene
blurb: This coastal scene, probably in Italy, has people on the beach enjoying the sunshine. The buildings in the mid-foreground at the water’s edge have their roofs silhouetted against the hills in the background. The composition denotes a sense of design and spatial organisation of this undoubtedly talented artist and who was a master at selecting interesting locations in which to set up his easel.

title: Doorway of a Church, Italy
subject: Streetscape
blurb: This watercolour painted in Italy has the Church doorway as the focal point with powerful, emblematic architecture depicted with interpretive lines sufficient for the Classical elements to be clearly read but in an Impressionistic manner. The composition has form and colour and is bathed in the brilliant sunlight of Italy and part in shadow. The element of spontaneity has been fully integrated into the artist process in the form of the figures, each of which has individuality and each telling a human story. One has the feeling of visually eavesdropping on the conversations taking place such is the power of the emotions stirred up by the artist.

title: Albenga, Italy
subject: Streetscape
blurb: Whatever clues to artistic technique Knighton-Hammond had managed to glean for himself living in the South of France and Italy between 1922 and 1932, the tuition that he received at Manchester Municipal School of Art under Adolphe Valette just before WW1, gave him a firm sense of direction towards Impressionism. This watercolour of Albenga in Italy, like most of K-H’s continental street and market scenes, can be described as a celebration of urban life. The tall, imposing buildings are a mastery of perspective and are a testament to the technical virtuosity of his draughtsmanship. The busy figures in their clusters, reveal human stories being told and bringing movement and life to the work which is certainly one of the most necessary tasks of the true artist. K-H masters this along with showing his potential as a colourist and amply demonstrates his compositional strength.

title: Washing by the river
subject: Landscape
blurb: The figures appear to be washing clothes in the river experiencing the brilliant light and colour of the riviera. The buildings on the far river bank are bathed in sunlight and depicted in an impressionist manner. The spontaneity of the figures, which have individuality, bring life to the composition. The subtle tonal manipulation gives recession and was essential to the success of the picture. The setting may well have been the Torrente Nervia in Liguria, Italy.

title: The Cottage at Kimmeridge
subject: Coastal Scene
blurb: The Cottage at Kimmeridge is perched on a hill overlooking the bay. The composition is in soft textured pastel with the colours blended with the artist’s figure tips. He has adopted colour bands to describe the sky, ranging from white, pink, green and blue. The sea is similarly composed with the colours of the sea and the reflected sky. The buildings are outlined with soft blurred edges silhouetted against the sea.

title: Landscape with trees
subject: Landscape
blurb: This landscape is dominated by the large tree. The elements of nature benefit from the texture of the pastel by creating the effect of tangible foliage. The landscape is layered in bands of colour as it recedes into the distance. The artist makes full use of the coloured paper on which he has laid down the pastel. The patches of bare paper form part of the colour scheme for the sky. There is little doubt that this picture was rapidly sketched and one can sense the improvisation of the texture and the transitions of hue as the scene evolved before the artist.

title: Barges on the Thames
subject: Cityscape
blurb: Barges on the Thames, painted in pastel, a medium which suited Knighton-Hammond as he could work rapidly fix the scene when he first encountered it. The granular softness of the stick of pastel allowed him apply texture and to blur the edges of both object and reflection in the composition. The boats have skilful foreshortening. The bridges receding into the distance give depth to this colourful picture.

title: Self portrait
subject: Portrait
blurb: This self-portrait of the artist shows acute observation probably looking in a mirror. The focus is on the eyes looking out at the spectator. The light source is from the sitters left and the pastels have modelled the head to reflect this. The artist’s spectacles are particularly well depicted. The collar and tie have been detailed whereas the jacket is minimal and fades out. The background is limited to an area which helps in defining the outline of the head. Knighton-Hammond was to carry out many more self-portraits in later life.

title: Cattle in landscape
subject: Landscape
blurb: The landscape with cattle shows Knighton-Hammond’s continued interest in the variety landscapes can offer. The changing moods and shifting lights are reflected in the change of tones. The texture of the pastel explores the panoramic structure and has minimal narrative with only the cattle in the foreground providing the motif and bringing life and movement to the picture.

title: Kent
subject: Landscape
blurb: A landscape study in Kent dominated by the motifs of the trees and a corn stook. The variety in the landscape was evidently of interest to Knighton-Hammond. This picture has depth through the successive planes – the foreground field, the trees, the distant landscape and the sky. Simple in form yet effective in relation to the whole composition.

title: Landscape with trees
subject: Landscape
blurb: This very atmospheric landscape has only the near foreground in local colour. The trees are silhouetted against what appears to be an ever-changing sky. The clouds would have been formed on the paper by rapid notation with the brush. The four distinct colour planes, including the intense blue, give clever aerial recession to the composition.

title: The Hills above Nice
subject: Landscape
blurb: The view of The Hills above Nice is provided with a vista through an avenue of trees which leads one’s eye into the composition to the hills beyond. Light here is the principal agent – the brilliant light of the Mediterranean – impacting on the colours washed with watercolour exploiting the subtle qualities evoking the brightness of the day.

title: West Bay
subject: Coastal Scene
blurb: Knighton-Hammond has conjured the atmosphere of the harbour at West Bay from fine, misty colour washes and the changing effects of the sky which he would not have considered merely a background such was the importance he placed on this light source. The harbour is silhouetted against the sea and sky. The two figures walking along the seafront give a sense of scale and movement to the composition.

title: The Barns at Ditchling
subject: Landscape
blurb: This watercolour, painted in Ditchling, is Knighton-Hammond using a very limited palette and has the confidence to draw the composition directly in watercolour – no pencil under drawing. It is a watercolour of great freedom but on close observation painted with great accuracy – very typical of K-H. The steeply pitched roof in the background of the buildings is the spire of Saint Margaret’s Church and farm buildings in the foreground.

title: Thatched houses in Worcestershire
subject: Streetscape
blurb: Thatched historic buildings on the side of the road in Great Comberton, Worcestershire, have been quickly sketched with the etching needle into the wax on the copper plate. The trees have been similarly depicted drawn at speed. A shepherd driving his sheep along the road gives movement and scale to the composition. The shadows create a mood in the etching.

title: Portrait of a young woman
subject: Portrait
blurb: A striking and colourful portrait of a young woman looking thoughtfully into space and towards the light source. There is a fresh expression in the modelling of the face. The golden locks capture the light and the clothing depicted in oil paint has texture and vibrance. One has the feeling that Knighton-Hammond had in his mind when painting this portrait Botticelli’s portrayal of Simonetta Vespucci, the image used by the artist in his Birth of Venus and Primavera. As always K-H captures the character of the sitter. Whilst the portrait is unsigned there is no doubt this is the work of Knighton-Hammond and has also been certified as such in an inscription verso by the artist's daughter.

title: Portrait of a woman
subject: Portrait
blurb: A striking portrait of a young woman confidently posing looking directly at the artist and as such the spectator. The face is superbly modelled with impasto oil paint. There is the hint of a smile probably as a response to the artist working away behind his easel. Whilst the portrait is unsigned there is no doubt this is the work of Knighton-Hammond and has also been certified as such in an inscription verso by the artist's daughter.

title: Coastal scene
subject: Coastal Scene
blurb: A lively coastal scene in the South of France. The figures provide great movement and spontaneity to the composition. The mature tree dominates the mid-foreground and the mountains which surround the coast form the background. The buildings provide the linear perspective and scale set within the aerial perspective which the artist cleverly creates to provide depth. An impressionist picture which Knighton-Hammond would have painted at lightning speed.

title: A view of the bay
subject: Coastal Scene
blurb: A view from the hills of a coast town on a rainy day. The foreground is full of local colour of the green foliage in the grass and bushes and trees in browns. In the mid-foreground there are sheep grazing in the fields. The town within the bay is picked out in the atmospheric blue colours resulting from the veil of atmosphere created by distance and the effects of the rain. This early picture shows the artist has mastered the difficult art of aerial perspective creating depth within the composition.

title: Roman Bridge at Sospel
subject: Landscape
blurb: This watercolour is one of a number of paintings of the famous Roman Bridge at Sospel up in the Maritime Alps. Knighton-Hammond would have set himself and his painting equipment up partly in the bed of the River Bevera to find the vantage point chosen for this scene. The bridge is imposing set against the alps. The picture is painted with great freedom and fluidity yet is accurate in the portrayal of the bridge and the architecture. The bridge was a favourite subject for many artists including Knighton-Hammond's friend, Sir Frank Brangwyn and his former master at Manchester Municipal School of Art, Adolphe Valette from whom he was greatly influenced.

title: G K Chesterton
subject: Portrait
blurb: This seated portrait of the writer and philosopher Gilbert Keith Chesterton (1874-1936) would have been undertaken in Ditchling. Chesterton was a frequent visitor to the town as his work was published by the Ditchling Press. He was a large man in both stature and in presence. Knighton-Hammond captures him in this etching comfortably seated in a relaxed pose. He has a philosophical gaze as he looks away from the spectator. There is an immediacy in the speed of the etching needle sketching on the copper plate to produce this powerful image.

title: A French Market Place
subject: Streetscape
blurb: A French Market place is a good example to demonstrate K-H at work. The picture is incomplete but helps us understand his style and technique. The figures, which are always on the move, are sketched in at lightning speed and a daub of colour added. The semi-permanent market stalls are outlined in watercolour. The majestic architecture follows without the urgency of the rest of the composition being permanent. The figures in outline and the handcart and dog are awaiting the addition of colour but still provide the spontaneity and shows the skill of the artist’s draughtsmanship. K-H shows his skill to exploit the special ability of watercolour to convey light and space.

title: The Abbey Church Yard and Grand Pump Room, Bath, 1919
subject: Streetscape
blurb: This watercolour of the Abbey Churchyard in Bath was painted in 1919 whilst Knighton-Hammond was on a break from British Dyes. The artist would have set himself up with the west main entrance of the abbey. The building to the left is the north façade of Grand Pump Room completed in 1706, ahead beyond the columnar screen fronting Stall Street was the Grand Pump Room Hotel which was built in 1869 and to the right was shops. Outside the Grand Pump Room are sedan chairs waiting to provide a taxi service in a traditional Georgian manner. The figures are almost ghost like as they were sketched in with transparent watercolours giving movement and spontaneity. The Classical architecture is superbly depicted with remarkable precision with ‘Impressionist’ detail and fine perspective. Sunlight and shadow add to the richness of the honey-coloured Bath stone ashlar facades. It is clear that Knighton-Hammond was developing an interest in urban spaces with human activity. The Grand Pump Room Hotel was demolished in 1958 making way for a block of flats, Arlington House.

title: Mapledurham
subject: Streetscape
blurb: This street scene in Mapledurham is a colourful and charming watercolour. Amongst the figures in the street a young girl is playing with her hoop. The boundary walls and buildings provide the linear perspective with the spectator’s eye being drawn to the church towards the vanishing point. The trees and bushes add colour to the composition. Painted on the spot the watercolour has great freshness and immediacy.

title: The Bent Tree
subject: Landscape
blurb: The Bent Tree stands somewhat precariously in the fence line. Other bows of the tree have been lost. The timber fence forms the demarcation in the fields. The hill on the horizon has cattle grazing. The artist has used a limited palette focusing on greens and browns but the gradation of the tones of the greens makes for convincing foliage and gives depth from foreground to background.

title: The South Downs
subject: Landscape
blurb: This extensive landscape of the South Downs in Sussex has K-H working in a very fluid manner in watercolours. He has a large tree at close quarters to where he set up his paints and further trees in the mid foreground with some buildings beyond. The clouds are bleak with no sign of blue skies. The composition has the artist working with great freedom and at speed.

title: The trees on Bale's Hill
subject: Landscape
blurb: The trees on Bale’s Hill, Bale’s Farm in Misterton is a well-known landmark and featured in many pictures by K-H. The watercolour depicts the trees on the hill with the horizon beyond. In the main the composition is a cloud study. K-H was well skilled in painting clouds where the rapid notation of the ever-moving subject suited the speed at which he worked.

title: The Peak District
subject: Landscape
blurb: An atmospheric landscape probably in the Peak District with a hillside and a lone tree. The artist uses the local green colour for the foreground foliage and as we move towards the background the atmospheric blue takes over giving aerial perspective and depth. K-H demonstrates his skill with the rapid notation of the clouds adding further to the atmosphere.

title: Brecon 1909
subject: Landscape
blurb: This watercolour is inscribed 'Evening sketch at Brecon 1909' and has the artist set up on the river bank focusing on the bridge and town beyond. The buildings of Brecon are constructed in grey Welsh stone and slate and the scene is dominated by the prominent church rising above the roof lines.

title: The Moorings
subject: Coastal Scene
blurb: A very freely painted watercolour of sailing boats moored up against the harbour walls. The horizon is very atmospheric and there is tranquility in the scene with the calmness of the water. The artist clearly liked this picture as he gave it to his daughter as can be seen in the inscription 'To my darling Mary'.

title: A Street in Grimaldi
subject: Streetscape
blurb: K-H's instinctive feeling for light, colour and tone is demonstrated in this luminous watercolour of a street in Grimaldi, a town close to the Franco/Italian border. The scene has freshness and immediacy, the finely depicted building bathed in dappled sunlight and the passing figures painted at speed to create a sense of movement. The artist has maximised the qualities of watercolour to convey light and space in an impressionistic style.

title: Figures before a Church
subject: Streetscape
blurb: ‘Figures before a Church’ was possibly painted in Menton and shows K-H at his Continental best. With the architectural features quickly sketched in with the brush, there is little detail apparent at close quarters yet when viewed from a distance the impressionism kicks in so that the composition can be fully read and understood. The figures have been sketched in outline at lightning speed with the brush before being in-filled with watercolour wash to give transparency and a feeling of spontaneity and movement. The day’s trading is coming to a close and the horse and cart are about to set off. The composition is enlivened by the artist’s signature use of red slashes in the clothing. These Continental watercolours set K-H apart from his contemporaries so much so that Augustus John rightly declared him to be ‘the greatest English painter in watercolours of our time’.

title: The Collegiate Church of Notre Dame, Eu, Normandy
subject: Streetscape
blurb: The Collegiate Church of Notre Dame in Eu, Normandy was undergoing restoration when K-H painted it. A hoarding and scaffolding had been erected to part of the façade and a workman can be seen climbing a ladder. The clusters of figures conversing and going about their business are painted with great spontaneity. The architecture of the church, particularly the tracery of the windows, is well depicted. The composition is enhanced by the splash of greenery in the background with the foreground in deep shadow.

title: A Passing Shower
subject: Landscape
blurb: Knighton-Hammond’s character studies were not confined to portraits. The cattle grazing scene has the central cow lying down and looking out at the artist or spectator with an interesting expression on it’s face. The three others are happily grazing away in the field. The passing showers create atmosphere sufficient for the hills in the background to take on an atmospheric blue colour. The colour of the trees is also impacted by the veil of atmosphere left by the passing rain. In later life Knighton-Hammond enjoyed going out into the fields to paint. He was drawn to painting cattle and these always made for interesting compositions. This study of cattle would have been painted at speed in watercolour giving the feel of movement to the animals.

title: Fishing boat with figures
subject: Coastal Scene
blurb: Figures sitting on benches beside a beached fishing vessel. The figures are in conversation. This would have been a rapid drawing onto the etching plate in quite an attacking style.

title: Resting
subject: Landscape
blurb: The three horses are resting and are painted very freely in watercolour. This picture is an example of Knighton-Hammond’s skill in the art as when viewed close to the composition does not appear structured but when viewed from a distance the picture transforms into a bright and colourful scene.

title: Entrance to a castle
subject: Landscape
blurb: Shepherdess and sheep grazing at the entrance to a castle is an early watercolour. The masonry of the castle facade is depicted in sunshine and shadow. The figure and sheep give movement to the tranquil scene.

title: Sailing Boats at Concarneau
subject: Coastal Scene
blurb: The sailing boats in the harbour at Concarneau are painted in the bright, fresh colours of Northern France. The elements of the composition - the architecture and boats - are painted with great freedom and great accuracy. The spontaneous figures on the far side of the harbour make for a busy scene. The buildings and boats are beautifully reflected in the calm waters of the harbour.

title: John, the artist's son
subject: Portrait
blurb: A portrait of the artist's son, John. Executed in watercolour and painted in a very free manner. The light is coming from the spectator's left which aids the modelling of the head. This would have been a very quick portrait and there are signs of pencil drawing in the outline of the face. John is smartly dressed in jacket and tie. We know Knighton-Hammond enjoyed painting portraits of his family.

title: Flower study
subject: Flower Study
blurb: A study of flowers in a blue vase delicately and skilfully depicted in fresh watercolours. The vase appears to be placed on an upside-down flowerpot and with the shadows it may well have been painted out of doors. There is no precision to the arrangement, so it was likely that Mrs Knighton-Hammond was not involved in the preparation of the display. The artist preferred less formal compositions of flowers for his studies. The picture was exhibitioned at the Chichester House Gallery, Ditchling in May 1976.

title: Brighton Beach
subject: Coastal Scene
blurb: Brighton Beach has multiple figures sitting amongst the small sailing boats on the beach. The buildings forming the streetscape have been painted at great speed. The artist has used a limited palette of colours to good effect creating an interesting composition. The watercolour was exhibited at Manchester Academy of Fine Arts in 1946 where it was purchased by Maxwell Reekie, an art agent acting on behalf of the National Gallery of South Africa, for their permanent collection. Reproduced by kind permission of the National Gallery of South Africa, Cape Town

title: Cornstooks in a landscape
subject: Landscape
blurb: Landscape with cornstooks shows competence in the art of aerial perspective. The rich greens and yellows of the foreground recede into the hazy blues in the atmospheric background hills. There is a reflective lake in the centre ground. Perspective is assisted by the farm building.

title: Shepherd and his flock
subject: Landscape
blurb: The Shepherd and his flock would have been a later picture by the artist. His style had an air of urgency in the brushstrokes. The sheep are wandering in the long grass and the shepherd looks on. This was probably Mr Jeffrey with his sheep. There is stormy weather in the distance.

title: Plum Cottage, Woodford, Cheshire
subject: Landscape
blurb: This cottage is Plum Cottage in Woodford, Cheshire. A much painted building which Knighton-Hammond clearly was very fond of. The figure of a woman carrying a bucket in each hand is walking towards the cottage. The church in the background and the trees make for a very pleasant country scene.

title: Willy Lott's House
subject: Landscape
blurb: Willy Lott’s House is in Flatford, East Bergholt in Suffolk. The building is most famous for featuring in a number of paintings by John Constable, notably The Hay Wain. The cottage is on the River Stour and is downstream from Flatford Mill in the heart of Dedham Vale. Willy Lott was the tenant farmer at the time Constable was there painting. Knighton-Hammond would have been fully aware of the Constable connection with the cottage as he was a great admirer of Constable’s work. The artist uses light and colour to create this tranquil scene. The Stour is calm and reflective, the architecture of the cottage is well painted.

title: Wooded Landscape
subject: Landscape
blurb: Wooded landscape is an exercise in the art of depicting trees. There is a colour range for the different species of tree and light and shadow as one’s eye is drawn deeper into the wood.

title: Cornstooks
subject: Landscape
blurb: This painting of the cornstooks is in rich oil paint. This is an extensive landscape with hills in the background and effective aerial perspective has been achieved. The foreground cornstooks have been painted with thick paint giving texture to the elements of the composition.

title: Flower Market, Menton
subject: Streetscape
blurb: Flower Market, Menton has few colours but the yellow of the flowers in the market provides the main splash of colour. The figures in the foreground have been painted in a very spontaneous manner. The façade of the buildings forms the main feature of the picture. Painted with the minimum of detail yet sufficient for a full appreciation of the architecture.

title: Drying the Sails
subject: Coastal Scene
blurb: Drying the Sails would have been painted probably in Menton. There is an impressive façade to the building forming the central span of the picture with a backdrop of trees. The sails hanging out to dry are draped over the boats. The figures in the distance between the sails add movement and scale to the composition.

title: Jeffery's Farm
subject: Landscape
blurb: This farming scene would have been on Manor Farm, Misterton. Mr Jeffery, the farm owner, is depicted here with his sheep which have been cleverly captured by Knighton-Hammond with varying angles of foreshortening. This variety gives great movement to the picture. The background is dominated by large trees and fields beyond.

title: Cart horse and figures
subject: Landscape
blurb: The cart horse is the central focal point and one can sense the strength and power of the animal as it stands in readiness to pull the wagon. Two figures go about loading the wagon with their pitchforks. This would have been a rapidly painted watercolour just providing sufficient detail to bring reality and movement to the composition. The background is sketched in with colourwashes.

title: Stormy Day
subject: Landscape
blurb: The farm buildings bring perspective and thus depth to the picture. The figures in the middle ground give scale. A passing storm creates a veil of atmosphere to the middle and backgrounds.

title: Farmland
subject: Landscape
blurb: This large oil painting has two figures – a girl and a boy in the foreground with cattle spread into the distance. The background is made up of houses and farm buildings. A colourful, Autumn scene.

title: Mary and her mother on a seat
subject: Conversation Piece
blurb: Mary and Her Mother on a seat was painted in pastels during the artist and his family’s staying with architect friend Edgar Wood at his home in Monte Calvario, Porto Maurizio. Edgar Wood was an architect from Manchester who moved to a converted monastery before designing and building a new home nearby at Monte Calvario. Knighton-Hammond may well have known Wood from Manchester and during the late 1920s spent a good deal of time travelling from his home in Cap Martin to visit him. The ornate seat on which the artist’s wife Emmeline (second wife) is sitting with her daughter Mary was designed by Edgar Wood. This is one of a number of pictures of wife and daughter sitting on the seat. Wood was a very good exponent of the art of pastel painting and may well have introduced it to Knighton-Hammond. Here the artist has used the colour of the paper as well as the colours of the pastels to create the composition. If pastel painting was new to Knighton-Hammond he was an immediate success in the art.

title: Mary and her mother sitting on a seat
subject: Conversation Piece
blurb: Mary and Her Mother sitting on a seat was painted during the artist and his family’s staying with architect friend Edgar Wood at his home in Monte Calvario, Porto Maurizio. Edgar Wood was an architect from Manchester who moved to a converted monastery before designing and building a new home nearby at Monte Calvario. Knighton-Hammond may well have known Wood from Manchester and during the late 1920s spent a good deal of time travelling from his home in Cap Martin to visit him. The ornate seat on which the artist’s wife Emmeline (second wife) and daughter Mary are sitting was designed by Edgar Wood. This is one of a number of pictures of wife and daughter sitting on the seat. This would have been a very quick and fluid painting in a very impressionistic manner.

title: Bradford Dale, Derbyshire
subject: Landscape
blurb: Bradford Dale, Derbyshire is a picture that immediately draws the spectator’s eye along the river. In doing so you pick up the trees en-route before settling on the village in the background depictured in hazy blues created by the atmosphere.

title: Courtyard Gateway
subject: Landscape
blurb: Courtyard Gateway is a very precisely depicted composition. There is great detailing of the brickwork of the pillers forming the gateway and masonry of the boundary wall. One can fully appreciate the materials of the buildings. The figures are very Edwardian in the dress as they walk towards the gateway from the courtyard. The foliage in the foreground gives colour to this very fresh picture which would be approaching 120 years old!

title: Extensive landscape
subject: Landscape
blurb: Extensive landscape is a series of watercolour washes rapidly applied to create a picture of considerable depth. The green of the foreground recedes into the blue of the background – the change of colour created by the veil of atmosphere.

title: Lover's Leap, Buxton
subject: Landscape
blurb: Lover’s Leap, Buxton is Ashwood Dale and is a canyon formed by cliffs. The artist has set up at the base of the canyon to gain the full effects of the imposing cliffs on either side. The bed rocks run into the distance where the atmospheric colours take over. There is a freshness in the light-green foliage and a freshness from the light entering the deep canyon. There is an air of tranquillity about the composition.

title: Cottage in a flower garden
subject: Streetscape
blurb: Cottage in a flower garden makes for a very welcoming entrance to the property. The stonework to the boundary wall to the garden and gateway are well depicted and the flowers form a riot of colour as one proceeds into the garden. The cottage with its stone slate roof may well be a feature of Derbyshire vernacular architecture.

title: The Arts Club, Dover Street, London
subject: Interior Scene
blurb: Knighton-Hammond was a member of the Arts Club, Dover Street and would often attend during the 1930s. He enjoyed the company of fellow artists and couldn’t resist getting his sketchbook out. The interior scene was later transferred to the etching plate. This is the smaller of two etchings of the Arts Club Knighton-Hammond produced. In this scene there are only a couple of members present and they are busy reading books. Knighton-Hammond has left a considerable amount on ink in this plate which creates a darker more sombre interior.

title: The Arts Club, Dover Street, London
subject: Interior Scene
blurb: Knighton-Hammond was a member of the Arts Club, Dover Street and would often attend during the 1930s. He enjoyed the company of fellow artists and couldn’t resist getting his sketchbook out. The interior scene was later transferred to the etching plate. This is the larger of two etchings of the Arts Club Knighton-Hammond produced. His etching needle was working at speed in quite an attacking manner and there is a lot of ink in the foreground studies which reduces further into the picture. He captures the various conversation pieces taking place in the club. The artist was to later re-work the plate adding more to the background and produced a later state for the etching.

title: On the plage at Dieppe
subject: Coastal Scene
blurb: On the beach at Dieppe has figures under awnings shaded from the sun. A busy picture with the figures painted a speed amusing themselves with the various activities taking place. The picture was exhibited at the Royal Academy in 1930 as ‘The Plage at Dieppe’ (No. 713).

title: Knighton-Hammond self-portrait
subject: Portrait
blurb: This self-portrait is in oils has the artist’s eyes engaging with the spectator. Indeed, it is the eyes which draws one into the picture. Knighton-Hammond painted a number of self-portraits in various mediums. There is little doubt he was an accomplished portrait artist capturing his own character on this occasion.

title: A view through the trees to Cap Martin
subject: Coastal Scene
blurb: View through the trees to Cap Martin would not have taken Knighton-Hammond very long to paint. There is freedom in the brushwork creatively depicting the trees in the foreground. There would have been a quick colour wash for the sea and the peninsula of Cap Martin in the background. The sky has little cloud so again would have been a simple colour wash. Clever and effective.

title: Gladioli
subject: Flower Study
blurb: The bowl of gladioli is a colourful flower study in oils. His has used the texture of the paint to form the petals giving a three-dimensional quality. The artist has placed a small classical bust alongside the flowers to add to the interest.

title: Oriel Window, Haddon Hall
subject: Landscape
blurb: The Oriel Window, Haddon Hall is contained within the elevation of this major historic stately home. In his early days a young Arthur Hammond spent as much time as he could at Haddon Hall. He would paint scenes within the grounds, the exterior of the building and the interior. He would often sit alongside other artists working there to gain from their experience. The masonry features of the building are well executed, and colour is added from the flowers and foliage.

title: Family Gathering
subject: Family Gathering
blurb: A family gathering probably in the garden of Old Court, Misterton. Featured are Mrs Knighton-Hammond (third wife), the artist’s daughter Mary (by his second wife), stepdaughter Ann and Di Wright (nanny). Knighton-Hammond enjoyed painting family conversation pieces and this picture was painted at speed. There is sufficient detail in the faces (and the back of the head) to make the family member recognisable.

title: October Flowers
subject: Flower Study
blurb: Knighton-Hammond carried out a series of flower studies where he would paint whatever flowers he could for all months of the year. October features a variety of flowers painted in watercolour contained within a vase with classical figures around the perimeter. A colourful study which uses the paper as well as paint in the rendering of the flowers.

title: August Flowers
subject: Flower Study
blurb: Knighton-Hammond carried out a series of flower studies where he would paint whatever flowers he could for all months of the year. August features a variety of flowers painted in watercolour contained within a vase with cherubs on the front panel. A colourful study which uses the paper as well as paint in the rendering of the flowers.

title: Flower Market, Menton
subject: Streetscape
blurb: The Flower Market, Menton is a watercolour full of light and colour. The figures in the market in the foreground have been painted at great speed giving spontaneity and movement. Two trees stand proud in the square and the background shows off the architecture of the south of France.

title: The Casino at Monte Carlo. Early Evening
subject: Streetscape
blurb: The Casino in Monte Carlo, Early evening is a clever composition using artificial light. The façade of the casino has the impression that is it emitting light rather than just reflecting the artificial light being trained on it. The figures walking towards the casino and the trees are silhouetted against the light. The sky is a deep blue. A very powerful watercolour.

title: Menton 1928 - Mending the Nets
subject: Coastal Scene
blurb: Mending the nets, Menton 1928 is a solitary figure of a fisherman mending his nets in his boat. The figure is concentrating on the task in hand. This would have been a quick and freely painted watercolour.

title: Casino at Monte Carlo
subject: Streetscape
blurb: An extraordinary light and colourful watercolour of the Casino at Monaco. Figures are walking towards the spectator along a balustraded walkway. The urns on the balustrade are full of colourful flowers. Various species of trees obscure the view of the casino in the background. A very impressionist watercolour demonstrating the artist’s development in freedom of execution with great accuracy.

title: St Mark's Square, Venice
subject: Streetscape
blurb: The view of St Mark’s Square, Venice through two archways is a picture full of colour and the hustle and bustle of people. This picture would have been painted when Knighton-Hammond first visited Venice in 1922. There is great spontaneity about the figures spread throughout the piazza. The façade of San Marco is at the far side of the square. The building to the right gives depth to the picture with is accurate perspective. The arches show the classical detailing of the masonry structure.

title: Sussex Woodland
subject: Landscape
blurb: A Sussex Woodland is an etching with limited subject matter – just trees. The trees in the foreground have exposed roots giving a feeling of the power of nature. Going into the picture there is a disposition of space between the trees and also the hatching indicates light and shade on the trunks whilst giving the sense of roundness and solidity.

title: John in his study
subject: Interior Scene
blurb: This picture of John, the artist’s son, studying is an interplay of light and shadow. A comparatively dark interior with lighting entering in from the window. John is sitting on a chair at a writing slope penning a letter. A statue of a head stands over him towards the window. A clever composition in chiaroscuro.

title: Pott Shrigley
subject: Streetscape
blurb: This etching of a street scene in Pott Shrigley is well executed with regards to perspective. The cottages are drawn and start the journey of the spectator’s eye being drawn down the road, passing the shepherd and sheep until you reach the church. The architecture and trees are well depicted. The shepherd and sheep and the chickens in the foreground add to the movement of the picture. The artist did not lose any of the spontaneity of the original drawing when transferred onto the etching plate.

title: The Steps, Haddon Hall
subject: Landscape
blurb: The steps at Haddon Hall give access from the terrace of the Winter Garden down to the Upper Garden of this historic stately home. The grand external steps rise up from the lawn up to the balustraded terrace. This is one of a number of watercolours undertaken by the artist of the steps at Haddon Hall. Painted in an era when the Knighton-Hammond was painting in a free and colourful manner.

title: Plum Blossom Cottage, Woodford
subject: Landscape
blurb: Plum Blossom Cottage was at Woodford in Cheshire. The thatched cottage has plum trees in the garden hence the name. This is one of a number of watercolours undertaken from the garden of the cottage. The picture is freely painted with a good play on light and shade.

title: A sailing boat in harbour
subject: Coastal Scene
blurb: The sailing boats in harbour are painted in oils and the palette appears a little subdued for Knighton-Hammond. The style of the clothing worn by the figures attending the boat would suggest this may have been painted on a trip to Tunisia. This may also account for the change in colours and tone.

title: A ship in harbour
subject: Coastal Scene
blurb: The location of the ship in harbour is possibly Oneglia at Imperia, Liguria. The sailing vessel is very impressively depicted with the sails at the ready for departure. The figures on the harbour give an idea of scale. The reflections in the water tend to indicate a choppy sea migrating into the harbour. The background buildings on the quayside are painted with suggestions of detail. A really colourful and freely painted picture.

title: Man in a boat
subject: Coastal Scene
